query: Context: we have written our own physics-based keyhole and melt-pool model for laser powder bed fusion (1070 nm fibre laser, Gaussian beam 1/e^2 radius 40-45 um, 75-400 W, 0.3-2.4 m/s) of AlSi10Mg and a hypereutectic Al-24.3Si-0.14Mg (wt%) blend. It uses Drude-Fresnel optics of the liquid from its measured electrical resistivity, a ray tracer for multiple reflections in the keyhole, an energy balance at a keyhole wall at the boiling point, and CALPHAD enthalpies. We are now adding Mg evaporation, a powder layer, a tilted keyhole whose shape comes from a point-by-point wall energy balance, and Marangoni melt flow, and we need sourced inputs. Question: (a) what is the measured thermal conductivity, as a function of temperature from room temperature to the solidus, of as-built laser powder bed fusion AlSi10Mg (laser flash diffusivity with density and heat capacity), and how does heat treatment change it? (b) the same for hypereutectic Al-Si alloys with 17-30 wt% Si (cast, spray formed, or LPBF Al-20Si / Al-25Si / A390), and for pure Si; (c) the dynamic viscosity of liquid Al and liquid Al-Si alloys (up to 25 wt% Si) against temperature, with reference correlations (e.g. Assael et al. 2006, J. Phys. Chem. Ref. Data) and the Arrhenius parameters; (d) the temperature coefficient of surface tension for Al-Si and AlSi10Mg melts, with and without oxygen. Give numbers, temperature ranges, methods, and DOIs with table or figure numbers.
task_summary: Measured Thermophysical Properties And Surface Tension Data For AlSi10Mg And Al‑Si Alloys Including Temperature Dependencies

info.name: create_plan
info.description:
Create a plan to construct a thorough and accurate answer.

Decompose the input task into a set of sub-objectives that need to
be met in order to form the answer. Subsequently, when working on solving
the query, you can focus on these objectives one by one. Note that the
`update_plan` tool allows you to change the objectives if needed.

In addition to the objectives you deem necessary, add one final objective
to call the `answer` tool with your final answer, so that you do not
forget to submit your answer.

plan_json.description:
A JSON string encoding an object with an "objectives" list;
never pass objectives separately.
Each objective should be a dictionary with the following keys:
- "id": (int) an integer id for the plan objective
- "objective": (str) a human readable description of the objective's goal
- "rationale": (str) a human readable rationale
    describing why this objective is necessary and appropriate for the query.
- "status": (str) updated task status, default to pending,
    one of: pending, in-progress, or completed.
    "pending" is yet to be started,
    "in-progress" is the current objective being solved,
    "completed" is successfully completed with acceptance criteria met.
- "result": (str|None) The result of the objective, default to None.
- "evaluation": (str|None) Description of why the objective result
    meets the criteria for being complete. Default to None.

info.name: create_artifact
info.description:
Create an artifact that can be used in the final answer, based on information
you have collected so far.

How it works: the full message history thus far is passed to another LLM,
along with the question and your description. The LLM is tasked to create
an artifact that matches your specifications, including a title, caption,
and markdown content. You drive the process by specifying the type and
describing what you want.

Only use this tool *after* you have gathered sufficient evidence or
information to create a new artifact. Do not call this tool in parallel
with tools that are searching for information or evidence that would be
necessary to create this artifact.

It is very helpful after calls to several search tools,
after calls to the `gather_evidence` tool, but it is not required.
However, it should be called before the `answer` tool at
least one time, but more may be given if specifically helpful for
the task, so that the `answer` tool can use the artifacts for the answer.

An artifact can be any string representable fact or list of facts,
formatted using markdown syntax. The artifact will be generated as one of
the following types:
- table: Markdown tables with rows and columns (e.g., findings, methods, molecules)
- code_block: Code snippets in fenced code blocks
- blockquote: Quoted text or important facts (using > prefix)
- image: AI-generated image (chart, diagram, or visualization)

Each artifact consists of:
- A short title (3-8 words) that names what the artifact contains
- A caption (1-2 sentences) describing what the artifact shows and why it's useful
- Markdown content in a single element type (validated automatically with retries if needed)
  For image type, content is a markdown image embed ``![title](data:image/png;base64,...)``,
  embedding the PNG directly as a base64 data URL.

artifact_type.description:
Artifact type to create. Must be one of: table,
code_block, blockquote, image.
artifact_type.title: Artifact Type

description.description:
Description of what you want in the artifact. Be specific
about what information should be included, how it should be organized,
and what columns/sections/content you want. This guides the summary LLM.
For image type, describe the visual you want generated in detail.
description.title: Description

info.name: view_images
info.description:
Retrieve images from a document.

Use this tool when you need to see figures, tables, or other visual content.
The tool works by asking a weaker LLM agent to scan through the document, looking for
visual content matching the query you provide. When the agent finds matches, it will
crop the page to the relevant region. It can be tasked to return multiple images,
if desired. Note that the weaker LLM may be worse at *understanding* images than
you, so double-check its conclusions about the returned images. It is also stateless,
i.e. it will not remember what you have asked it to find in the past.

Use this tool carefully. It is difficult to retrieve images, and the images
themselves will fill up your context window quickly. Here are some guidelines:
1. ALWAYS use this tool if the question explicitly mentions 'Table X' or 'Figure Y'.
   These questions require visual content and cannot be answered with text alone.
2. Use this tool as a fallback when gather_evidence fails repeatedly (2+ times
   returning 'No relevant evidence'). This suggests the answer may be in visual content.
3. When gather_evidence returns text mentioning 'see Figure X' or 'shown in Table Y',
   you should call this tool to examine that specific visual reference.
4. Only call this tool after directly inspecting relevant text with read_text
   to confirm the document likely contains the visual you need.
5. Don't use this tool in a broad-spectrum way (don't call on many documents
   just to see what might be relevant).
6. Never call this tool in parallel with itself.
7. Users like visual evidence, so call this tool at least once before answering so you
   can provide some image citations in the answer. Add this to your plan so you do not forget.
   For images to be presented to the user, they must be cited in the final answer after retrieval
   by this tool. You may ignore this instruction if the request is for the question is asking
   for a specific piece of information and is not an open-ended research question.
8. NEVER cite full-page images in your final answer, unless they are full-page panels figures or
   tables. Cite relevant cropped regions if available, otherwise consider calling this tool again
   to find a smaller region that answers the query.

query.description:
Query to search for visual content in the document. If you know the specific
figure/table/formula you are looking for, you can specify it here (e.g. "find me
Figure 3" or "extract the table on page 10"). You can also request based on content
(e.g. "find me all volcano plots of gene X" or "I need the formula for the growth rate").
You can even include explicit instructions for the LLM agent to follow (if helpful, not
necessarily required). The more specific and clear your query is here, the higher the

query.description:
The search query string. Supports complex boolean expressions, field-specific
searches, and query modifiers through operators. All configuration is done through
operators in the query string.
Query Syntax:
    Basic Search:
        Simple text automatically uses default EXPANSION[Relaxation] and COVERAGE[Contains]
        >>> "heart attack"

    Modified Search:
        Use operators to modify search behavior:
        >>> 'EXPANSION[None]COVERAGE[FullMatch]"exact phrase"'
        >>> 'EXPANSION[Concept]heart attack'

    Field Search:
        Specify fields using AREA operator:
        >>> 'AREA[InterventionName]aspirin'
        >>> 'AREA[Phase]PHASE3'

    Location Search:
        Use SEARCH operator for compound location queries:
        >>> 'cancer AND SEARCH[Location](AREA[LocationCity]Boston AND AREA[LocationState]Massachusetts)'

    Complex Boolean:
        Combine terms with AND, OR, NOT and parentheses:
        >>> '(cancer OR tumor) AND NOT (EXPANSION[None]pediatric OR AREA[StdAge]CHILD)'

    Date Ranges:
        Use RANGE to specify date ranges with formats like "yyyy-MM" or "yyyy-MM-dd".
        Note that MIN and MAX can be used for open-ended ranges:
        >>> AREA[ResultsFirstPostDate]RANGE[2015-01-01, MAX]

Operators:
    EXPANSION[type]: Controls term expansion
        - None: Exact match only, case and accent sensitive
        - Term: Includes lexical variants (plurals, spellings)
        - Concept: Includes UMLS synonyms
        - Relaxation: Relaxes adjacency requirements (default)
        - Lossy: Allows missing partial terms

    COVERAGE[type]: Controls text matching
        - FullMatch: Must match entire field
        - StartsWith: Must match beginning of field
        - EndsWith: Must match end of field
        - Contains: Must match part of field (default)

    AREA[field]: Specifies field to search
        - See Field Reference for available fields

    SEARCH[type]: Groups field searches
        - Location: Groups location-related fields
        - Study: Groups study-related fields

Usage Notes:
    - All search expressions are implicitly OR expressions
    - Operator precedence (highest to lowest): terms/source operators, NOT/context operators, AND, OR
    - Use quotes for exact phrase matching: "heart attack"
    - Use parentheses for grouping: (heart OR cardiac) AND attack
    - Use backslash to escape operators: \AND
    - Default expansion is EXPANSION[Relaxation]
    - Default coverage is COVERAGE[Contains]

Field Reference:
    High Priority Fields (weight >= 0.8):

info.name: gather_evidence
info.description:
Given a specific question, gather evidence from full-text of documents that have been retrieved by
previous tool calls.

Here is how the tool works: the provided question is posed to all texts retrieved thus far
by other tools. An LLM sees each text independently and is prompted to find information relevant
to the question.

That is, we sample evidence `e \sim LLM(prompt, text, q)` for each text. We only return pieces of
evidence `e` that are sufficiently relevant to the question; if the text is irrelevant, then `e`
is not included in the final response of this tool. Note that this LLM does not see the conversation
history thus far, only the question and each text. Note that it only sees text, no images or other
media from the contents (though tables and formulae may be parseable in some cases).

Think of this tool as an efficient way to deeply scan all retrieved documents for evidence. It
is complementary to the `read_text` tool, which can be used to directly inspect a subset of the
retrieved documents.

A valuable time to invoke this tool is after another tool finds potentially relevant documents.
Feel free to invoke this tool in parallel with other tools, but do not call this tool in parallel with itself.
Only invoke this tool when the document count is above zero, or this tool will be useless.

If you call this tool 2+ times and repeatedly get 'No relevant evidence found',
consider whether the answer might be in visual content (figures/tables) rather than text,
and use appropriate tools if available to access that content.

Once you receive evidence from this tool:

1. Read Carefully: Don't skim. The evidence may contain multiple similar terms
   or values—make sure you identify the RIGHT one.

2. For Comparative Questions: If the question asks "which X has greatest Y",
   check that the evidence includes information about ALL relevant X options, not
   just one or two. If you only see partial information, gather more evidence.

3. Check for Noise: Verify that numbers or terms aren't just metadata
   (page numbers, reference IDs, dates). Look for the value in meaningful
   scientific context.

4. Context Matters: A term appearing 71 times doesn't mean it's always the answer.
   Verify which occurrence actually answers the question asked.

If the evidence doesn't clearly answer the question, gather more evidence before
concluding. Don't guess based on partial information.

question.description: Specific question to gather evidence for.
question.title: Question

text_name_focus_list.description:
if there are known text names that are relevant to the question,
you can specify them here. This will ensure that the tool will look at these text names
first, and then look at the rest of the evidence. If left as `None`, an embedding
search will be performed on underlying content to find most relevant texts.
text_name_focus_list.title: Text Name Focus List

info.name: answer
info.description:
Submit your final answer to the user. You MUST call this tool on your final answer.
If you mark all objectives as completed but have not yet called this tool, then
the answer will not be submitted. Note that this tool should only be called once, as it
immediately terminates the run and submits the answer.

Write an answer based on the evidence from gather_evidence results in message history.
If the context provides insufficient information, provide a partial answer and explain
why it is partial (e.g. the question is currently an open question in the field,
you were unable to obtain certain papers, etc.).

For each part of your answer, indicate which sources most support it via citation IDs at
the end of sentences, like (pqac-0000ABCD).
You are only allowed to cite available context IDs, indicated in previous messages by "Context IDs that may be cited:".
## Valid citation examples, only use comma/space delimited parentheticals:

- (pqac-0000ABCD, pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000IJKL)

## Invalid citation examples:

- (pqac-0000ABCD and pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000ABCD;pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000ABCD-pqac-0000EFGH)
- pqac-0000ABCD and pqac-0000EFGH
- Example's work pqac-0000ABCD
- (pages pqac-0000ABCD)
- ![description](pqac-0000ABCD)
- ()

Do not concatenate citation ids, just use them as-is.

When writing your answer, embed artifacts if relevant artifacts have been previously
created by the `create_artifact` tool. To embed an artifact, simply include this in your
answer, on its own line and without any additional formatting (i.e. no backticks, code fences,
quotes, additional tags, etc.).
Always provide at least some introductory sentence or paragraph before referring to an artifact,
so that the artifact is properly contextualized.
Here is an example reference to an artifact with ID "artifact-XY":
<artifact id="artifact-XY"/>

Valid artifact IDs are indicated in previous messages by 'Artifact IDs that may be injected into the answer:'.


Double-check your answer:

1. Evidence Match: Re-read the specific evidence snippets you're citing. Does your
   answer actually match what they say? Don't rely on memory from 20+ messages ago.

2. For Comparative Questions ("which X has greatest/maximum/highest Y"):
   - Did you examine ALL options mentioned in the evidence?
   - Did you explicitly compare their values?
   - Example: If evidence mentions "Pancreatic: 0.92, Liver: 0.85, Lung: 0.78",
     verify you compared all three, not just two.

3. For Specific Value Questions ("How many", "What is the", specific terms):
   - Does the exact value you're stating appear in the evidence?
   - Are you extracting from the right context (not noise like page numbers)?

4. Sanity Check: Read your answer. Does it directly address what was asked?

Don't use Markdown image syntax like ![...](...) to reference media in your answer,
because media get automatically linked by the system based on your answer's citations.

Write in the style of a scientific article, with concise sentences and
coherent paragraphs. This answer will be used directly,
so do not add any extraneous information.

answer.description: valid answer, cited with citation IDs.
answer.title: Answer

Abstract:

Purpose
AlSi10Mg alloy is commonly used in laser powder bed fusion due to its printability, relatively high thermal conductivity, low density and good mechanical properties. However, the thermal conductivity of as-built materials as a function of processing (energy density, laser power, laser scanning speed, support structure) and build orientation, are not well explored in the literature. This study aims to elucidate the relationship between processing, microstructure, and thermal conductivity.


Design/methodology/approach
The thermal conductivity of laser powder bed fusion (L-PBF) AlSi10Mg samples are investigated by the flash diffusivity and frequency domain thermoreflectance (FDTR) techniques. Thermal conductivities are linked to the microstructure of L-PBF AlSi10Mg, which changes with processing conditions. The through-plane exceeded the in-plane thermal conductivity for all energy densities. A co-located thermal conductivity map by frequency domain thermoreflectance (FDTR) and crystallographic grain orientation map by electron backscattered diffraction (EBSD) was used to investigate the effect of microstructure on thermal conductivity.


Findings
The highest through-plane thermal conductivity (136 ± 2 W/m-K) was achieved at 59 J/mm3 and exceeded the values reported previously. The in-plane thermal conductivity peaked at 117 ± 2 W/m-K at 50 J/mm3. The trend of thermal conductivity reducing with energy density at similar porosity was primarily due to the reduced grain size producing more Al-Si interfaces that pose thermal resistance. At these interfaces, thermal energy must convert from electrons in the aluminum to phonons in the silicon. The co-located thermal conductivity and crystallographic grain orientation maps confirmed that larger colonies of columnar grains have higher thermal conductivity compared to smaller columnar grains.


Practical implications
The thermal properties of AlSi10Mg are crucial to heat transfer applications including additively manufactured heatsinks, cold plates, vapor chambers, heat pipes, enclosures and heat exchangers. Additionally, thermal-based nondestructive testing methods require these properties for applications such as defect detection and simulation of L-PBF processes. Industrial standards for L-PBF processes and components can use the data for thermal applications.


Originality/value
To the best of the authors’ knowledge, this paper is the first to make coupled thermal conductivity maps that were matched to microstructure for L-PBF AlSi10Mg aluminum alloy. This was achieved by a unique in-house thermal conductivity mapping setup and relating the data to local SEM EBSD maps. This provides the first conclusive proof that larger grain sizes can achieve higher thermal conductivity for this processing method and material system. This study also shows that control of the solidification can result in higher thermal conductivity. It was also the first to find that the build substrate (with or without support) has a large effect on thermal conductivity.

Abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    Selective laser melting (SLM) offers considerable potential for fabricating thin-walled radiators because of its capability to produce lightweight components with complex structures. Among candidate materials, the AlSi10Mg alloy is particularly well suited for additive manufacturing (AM) due to its excellent processability. However, the rapid solidification inherent to the AM process leads to forming a supersaturated solid solution in the AlSi10Mg matrix, which markedly reduces its thermal conductivity. In this study, an aging heat treatment was employed to promote the precipitation of solute phases from the supersaturated solid solution, thereby enhancing the thermal conductivity and mechanical properties of the AlSi10Mg alloy. The results indicate that aging at 200 °C for 10 h effectively promotes the precipitation of Si particles within the α-Al matrix. This treatment yields a notable tensile strength of 350 MPa and a high thermal conductivity of 173.70 W·m⁻

                    <jats:sup>1</jats:sup>
                    , representing a 44.3% improvement over the as-built state. Thus, we achieved a synergistic enhancement of both thermal and mechanical properties. The improved thermal conductivity is attributed to reduction of solid-solution Si in the matrix and the refinement of precipitated Si particles. These findings provide both theoretical insights and technical guidance for fabricating high-performance aluminum alloy heat sinks via AM, with promising applications in aerospace and electronic cooling systems.

Abstract:
In the context of rising power densities in electrical machines, additive manufacturing presents an opportunity to develop more powerful thermal solutions. However, the physical properties of objects manufactured using this process remain unclear. This research examines the directional thermal and electrical conductivities of aluminum alloy (AlSi10Mg) and silicon steel (Fe-3.7%wt. Si) samples produced via laser powder bed fusion (LPBF), both prior to and following heat treatment. The findings indicate that the as-built aluminum samples exhibit higher conductivities in the orientation parallel to the LPBF build direction, while annealing results in higher conductivities overall and an absence of anisotropy. On the other hand, the silicon steel samples show constant conductivities and lack of anisotropy both before and after heat treatment. These results have practical applications in the design of additively manufactured electrical machines, where the thermal and electrical resistance of the materials have a major impact on thermal and electromagnetic performance.

Abstract:
Tailoring heat treatments for Laser Powder Bed Fusion (LPBF) processed materials is critical to ensure superior and repeatable material properties for high-end applications. This tailoring requires in-depth understanding of the LPBF-processed material. Therefore, the current study aims at unravelling the threefold interrelationship between the process (LPBF and heat treatment), the microstructure at different scales (macro-, meso-, micro-, and nano-scale), and the macroscopic material properties of AlSi10Mg. A similar solidification trajectory applies at different length scales when comparing the solidification of AlSi10Mg, ranging from mould-casting to rapid solidification (LPBF). The similarity in solidification trajectories triggers the reason why the Brody-Flemings cellular microsegregation solidification model could predict the cellular morphology of the LPBF as-printed microstructure. Where rapid solidification occurs at a much finer scale, the LPBF microstructure exhibits a significant grain refinement and a high degree of silicon (Si) supersaturation. This study has identified the grain refinement and Si supersaturation as critical assets of the as-printed microstructure, playing a vital role in achieving superior mechanical and thermal properties during heat treatment. Next, an electrical conductivity model could accurately predict the Si solute concentration in LPBF-processed and heat-treated AlSi10Mg and allows understanding the microstructural evolution during heat treatment. The LPBF-processed and heat-treated AlSi10Mg conditions (as-built (AB), direct-aged (DA), stress-relieved (SR), preheated (PH)) show an interesting range of superior mechanical properties (tensile strength: 300–450 MPa, elongation: 4–13%) compared to the mould-cast T6 reference condition.

Abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>This paper investigates the effects of surface friction stir treatment on the microstructure and defects of LPBF-produced AlSi10Mg alloy. Experimental analyses, supported by numerical simulations, investigate the effects of process conditions on material flow, strain distribution, resulting stir zone (SZ) characteristics, and overall microstructural transformations. The analytical investigation, coupled with statistical analysis, aims to define the links between imposed process conditions, effects on heat generation, heat diffusion, and material flow, and resulting material response in terms of microstructure and microhardness. Nine samples were treated using a pinless rotating tool under identical fabrication conditions. The treatment induced complete dynamic recrystallisation and significant softening within the SZ, with depths ranging from 1213 to 1617 μm, showing good agreement with numerical predictions. Numerical results delineated the origin of the characteristic vortexes as portions of material with the highest level of softening and demonstrated the effects of the processing parameters on their final position within the SZ. A reduction of approximately 30% in porosity and lack-of-fusion defects was achieved in the SZ. Microhardness decreased to 59.58 HV in the SZ and 65.27 HV in the TMAZ compared to 127.12 HV in the as-built material. The SZ depth and softening were strongly dependent on process parameters and were, within the analytical investigations, successfully correlated with dimensionless numbers, including the Péclet number, mechanical Reynolds number, and non-dimensional energy input. Abstract:
<jats:p>The development of advanced energy materials is critical for the safety and efficiency of next-generation nuclear energy systems. Aluminum alloys present a compelling option due to their excellent neutronic properties, notably a low thermal neutron absorption cross-section. However, their historically poor high-temperature performance has limited their use in commercial power reactors. This makes them prime candidates for specialized, lower-temperature but high-radiation environments, such as research reactors, spent fuel storage systems, and spallation neutron sources. In these applications, mitigating radiation damage—particularly swelling and embrittlement from helium produced during irradiation—remains a paramount challenge. Grain Boundary Engineering (GBE) is a potent strategy to mitigate radiation damage by increasing the fraction of low-energy Coincident Site Lattice (CSL) boundaries. These interfaces act as effective sinks for radiation-induced point defects (vacancies and self-interstitials), suppressing their accumulation and subsequent clustering into damaging dislocation loops and voids. By controlling the defect population, GBE can substantially reduce macroscopic effects like volumetric swelling and embrittlement, enhancing material performance in harsh radiation environments. In this article we evaluate the efficacy of GBE in an AlSi10Mg alloy, a candidate material for nuclear applications. Samples were prepared via KOBO extrusion, with a subset undergoing subsequent annealing to produce varied initial grain sizes and grain boundary character distributions. This allows for a direct comparison of how these microstructural features influence the material’s response to helium ion irradiation, which simulates damage from fission and fusion reactions. The resulting post-irradiation defect structures and their interaction with the engineered grain boundary network were characterized using a combination of Transmission Electron Microscopy (TEM) and High-Resolution Transmission Electron Microscopy (HRTEM), providing crucial insights for designing next-generation, radiation-tolerant energy materials.</jats:p>

Abstract:
This study investigated the impact of low-temperature heat treatments on the mechanical and thermophysical properties of Cu-10Sn alloys fabricated by a laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) additive manufacturing (AM) process. The microstructure, phase structure, and mechanical and thermal properties of the LPBF Cu-10Sn samples were comparatively investigated under both the as-fabricated (AF) condition and after low-temperature heat treatments at 140, 180, 220, 260, and 300 °C. The results showed that the low-temperature heat treatments did not significantly affect the phase and grain structures of the Cu-10Sn alloys. Both pre- and post-treatment samples displayed consistent grain sizes, with no obvious X-ray diffraction angle shift for the α phase, indicating that atom diffusion of the Sn element is beyond the detection resolution of X-ray diffractometers (XRD). However, the 180 °C heat-treated sample exhibited the highest hardness, while the AF samples had the lowest hardness, which was most likely due to the generation of precipitates according to thermodynamics modeling. Heat-treated samples also displayed higher thermal diffusivity values than their AF counterpart. The AF sample had the longest lifetime of ~0.19 nanoseconds (ns) in the positron annihilation lifetime spectroscopy (PALS) test, indicating the presence of the most atomic-level defects.

Abstract:
The characteristic property of a liquid, discriminating it from a solid, is its fluidity, which can be expressed by a velocity field. The reaction of the velocity field on forces is enshrined in the transport parameter viscosity. In contrast, a solid reacts to forces elastically through a displacement field, the particles are trapped in their potential minimum. The flow in a liquid needs enough thermal energy to overcome the changing potential barriers, which is supported through a continuous rearrangement of surrounding particles. Cooling a liquid will decrease the fluidity of a particle and the mobility of the neighbouring particles, resulting in an increase of the viscosity until the system comes to an arrest. This process with a concomitant slowing down of collective particle rearrangements might already start deep inside the liquid state. The idea of the potential energy landscape provides an attractive picture for these dramatic changes. However, despite the appealing idea there is a scarcity of quantitative assessments, in particular, when it comes to experimental studies. Here we present results on a monatomic liquid metal through a combination of ab initio molecular dynamics, neutron spectroscopy and inelastic x-ray scattering. We investigated the collective dynamics of liquid aluminium to reveal the changes in dynamics when the high temperature liquid is cooled towards solidification. The results demonstrate the main signatures of the energy landscape picture, a reduction in the internal atomic structural energy, a transition to a stretched relaxation process and a deviation from the high-temperature Arrhenius behavior of the relaxation time. All changes occur in the same temperature range at about 1.4·Tmelting\documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$1.4 \cdot T_{melting}$$\end{document}, which can be regarded as the temperature when the liquid aluminium enters the landscape influenced phase and enters a more viscous liquid state towards solidification. The similarity in dynamics with other monatomic liquid metals suggests a universal dynamic crossover above the melting point.

Abstract:
We present a study of dynamic properties of liquid aluminum using density-functional theory within the local-density (LDA) and generalized gradient (GGA) approximations. We determine the temperature dependence of the self-diffusion coefficient as well the viscosity using direct methods. Comparisons with experimental data favor the LDA approximation to compute dynamic properties of liquid aluminum. We show that the GGA approximation induce more important backscattering effects due to an enhancement of the icosahedral short range order (ISRO) that impact directly dynamic properties like the self-diffusion coefficient. All these results are then used to test the Stokes-Einstein relation and the universal scaling law relating the diffusion coefficient and the excess entropy of a liquid.

Abstract:
Liquid phase diffusion plays a critical role in phase transformations (e.g. glass transformation and devitrification) observed in marginal glass forming systems such as Al-Sm. Controlling transformation pathways in such cases requires a comprehensive description of diffusivity, including the associated composition and temperature dependencies. In the computational study reported here, we examine atomic diffusion in Al-Sm liquids using ab initio molecular dynamics (AIMD) and determine the diffusivities of Al and Sm for selected alloy compositions. Non-Arrhenius diffusion behavior is observed in the undercooled liquids with an enhanced local structural ordering. Through assessment of our AIMD result, we construct a general formulation for Al-Sm liquid, involving a diffusion mobility database that includes composition and temperature dependence. A Volmer-Fulcher-Tammann (VFT) equation is adopted for describing the non-Arrhenius behavior observed in the undercooled liquid. The composition dependence of diffusivity is found quite strong, even for the Al-rich region contrary to the sole previous report on this binary system. The model is used in combination with the available thermodynamic database to predict specific diffusivities and compares well with reported experimental data for 0.6 at.% and 5.6 at.% Sm in Al-Sm alloys.

Abstract:
In this paper, single-layer and bulk 316 L selective laser melting (SLM) experiments were conducted, fine submicron-scale geometric symmetrical cellular (hexagonal, pentagonal and square), elongated cellular and bands solidification morphologies were found in the laser-melt top surface. Meanwhile, morphological developed sub-grain patterns with quasi-hexagonal cellular, elongated cellular and bands structures (size ~1 μm) coexisting inside one single macro-solidified grain were also identified. This demonstrated the transitions from quasi-hexagonal-cells to elongated cells/bands, and transitions reverse, occurred in the whole bulk under some circumstances during SLM. Based on the experimental realities, these morphologies are formed by the local convection and Bénard instabilities in front of the solid/liquid interface (so-called mushy zones) affected by intricate temperature and surface tension gradients. Quasi-hexagonal cellular convective fields are then superimposed on macro-grain solidification to form the sub-grain patterns and micro-segregations. This explanation seems reasonable and is unifying as it can be expanded to other eutectic alloys with face center cubic (FCC) prevenient phase prepared by SLM, e.g., the Al-Si and Co-Cr-Mo systems.

Abstract:
ABSTRACT This paper focuses on the effect of melting modes on microstructural evolution and tribological properties of AlSi10Mg alloy fabricated by selective laser melting (SLM). The results showed that the microstructures of SLM AlSi10Mg consisted of primary α-Al surrounded by cellular Si networks (∼500 nm) when fabricated in conduction mode, but has a finer cellular-like Si phase (∼200 nm) when fabricated in keyhole mode. The strong convection caused by the melt reflow and Marangoni convection under keyhole mode also resulted in deposition of nano-scale Si particles at the bottom of the molten pool. The SLM AlSi10Mg fabricated in keyhole mode exhibited better wear resistance than that fabricated in conduction mode. Compared to traditional as-cast specimens, both SLM specimens showed better wear resistance due to the unique cellular-like networks. The SLM technique offers a new approach for material processing that can be used to refine microstructures for improved tribological properties.

## 5. Precise control of thermal conductivity at the nanoscale through individual phonon-scattering barriers.

@article{pernot2010precisecontrolof,
    author = "Pernot, G. and Stoffel, M. and Savić, I. and Pezzoli, F. and Chen, Peixuan and Savelli, G. and Jacquot, A. and Schumann, J. and Denker, U. and Mönch, I. and Deneke, C. and Schmidt, O. and Rampnoux, J. and Wang, Shidong and Plissonnier, M. and Rastelli, A. and Dilhaire, S. and Mingo, N.",
    title = "Precise control of thermal conductivity at the nanoscale through individual phonon-scattering barriers.",
    year = "2010",
    journal = "Nature materials",
    volume = "9 6",
    pages = "491-5",
    month = "Jun",
    doi = "10.1038/nmat2752",
    url = "https://doi.org/10.1038/nmat2752",
    publisher = "Springer Science and Business Media LLC",
    issue = "6",
    issn = "1476-1122"
}


Abstract:
The ability to precisely control the thermal conductivity (kappa) of a material is fundamental in the development of on-chip heat management or energy conversion applications. Nanostructuring permits a marked reduction of kappa of single-crystalline materials, as recently demonstrated for silicon nanowires. However, silicon-based nanostructured materials with extremely low kappa are not limited to nanowires. By engineering a set of individual phonon-scattering nanodot barriers we have accurately tailored the thermal conductivity of a single-crystalline SiGe material in spatially defined regions as short as approximately 15 nm. Single-barrier thermal resistances between 2 and 4 x 10(-9) m(2) K W(-1) were attained, resulting in a room-temperature kappa down to about 0.9 W m(-1) K(-1), in multilayered structures with as little as five barriers. Such low thermal conductivity is compatible with a totally diffuse mismatch model for the barriers, and it is well below the amorphous limit. The results are in agreement with atomistic Green's function simulations.

Richard R.J. Sélo, Sam Catchpole-Smith, Ian Maskery, Ian Ashcroft, and Christopher Tuck. On the thermal conductivity of alsi10mg and lattice structures made by laser powder bed fusion. Additive Manufacturing, 34:101214, Aug 2020. URL: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.addma.2020.101214, doi:10.1016/j.addma.2020.101214. This article has 204 citations and is from a highest quality peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt establishes that LPBF AlSi10Mg has anisotropic thermal conductivity in the as-built state and that heat treatment increases conductivity by modifying the alloy’s microstructure, particularly by breaking down the Si cellular structure. The only numerical as-built values provided are 119 ± 5 W·m−1·K−1 in the build direction and 103 ± 5 W·m−1·K−1 in the transverse direction; the excerpt does not specify a temperature range or provide a temperature-dependent conductivity curve from room temperature to the solidus. These values are reported in connection with EOS data, and the excerpt does not confirm that they were measured by laser flash diffusivity. It reports that annealing removes anisotropy and raises transverse conductivity by approximately 30%. A solution heat treatment raises conductivity by 36% relative to as-built, while a T6-like treatment produces the largest increase, 44%. The excerpt also states that heat-treated material reached 173 ± 10 W·m−1·K−1 in both directions. No specific results for stress-relief treatment or direct aging are included in the supplied pages, so their quantitative effects cannot be determined from this excerpt.

## pqac-00000001

From text 'liu2026synergisticenhancementof pages 2-5'.

Xiao Liu, Dong Yu, Yi-Ling Yuan, Jun-Jie Li, Zhi-Jun Wang, and Jin-Cheng Wang. Synergistic enhancement of thermal conductivity and mechanical properties of selective laser melting alsi10mg alloys via aging treatment. Jul 2026. URL: https://doi.org/10.1186/s40712-026-00540-8, doi:10.1186/s40712-026-00540-8. This article has 0 citations.

This excerpt describes room-temperature thermal-conductivity measurement for selective-laser-melted (LPBF/SLM) AlSi10Mg, rather than a temperature-dependent measurement extending from room temperature to the solidus. Thermal diffusivity was measured by laser flash analysis using an LFA 447 analyzer, with measurements taken along the deposition direction. Thermal conductivity was calculated from thermal diffusivity, specific heat capacity, and density; the specific heat capacity used was 0.88 J·g−1·°C−1, and five room-temperature measurements were averaged. The excerpt does not provide the numerical as-built thermal-conductivity value or a table/curve of values versus temperature, nor does it report solidus-temperature measurements. The investigated direct-aging treatments were 140, 160, 180, 200, and 220 °C for 10 hours, followed by air cooling. The rationale given is that aging can promote precipitation from the supersaturated solid solution, reduce solute-related electron scattering, and improve thermal conductivity while also strengthening the alloy. For comparisons from prior work, annealing reportedly produced the highest thermal conductivity among direct aging, annealing, and solution treatments in one study, while another study reported a 23.4% increase for directly aged material relative to the as-built state. Stress-relief and T6-specific quantitative changes are not provided in this excerpt.

Effects of processing parameters and heat treatment on thermal conductivity of additively manufactured alsi10mg by selective laser melting. Materials Characterization, 173:110945, Mar 2021. URL: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.matchar.2021.110945, doi:10.1016/j.matchar.2021.110945. This article has 99 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt establishes that the study measured thermal conductivity in selectively laser-melted (LPBF/SLM) AlSi10Mg and examined the effects of processing parameters, scanning strategies, porosity, and post-processing heat treatment. It reports that porosity significantly affects thermal conductivity. The specific quantitative heat-treatment result provided here is that annealing increased thermal conductivity by 18–41%, with no measurable change in porosity. The improvement was associated with microstructural evolution: silicon precipitation and coalescence increased with heat-treatment temperature, while dwell time had a smaller effect. The excerpt also notes that parts fabricated with the “points” scanning strategy, despite having more porosity than “contour-hatch” parts, could reach thermal conductivity values up to those of the contour-hatch strategy after heat treatment. It further indicates that acceptable thermal conductivity could be achieved at laser energy densities approximately one order of magnitude lower, for less mechanically demanding applications such as heat sinks. However, these pages do not provide the requested numerical thermal-conductivity values as a function of temperature from room temperature to the solidus, do not identify laser-flash diffusivity data, and do not report separate values for stress relief, T6, direct aging, and annealing. Those details must be obtained from later sections or another source.

After a 2 h heat treatment at 300 °C, conductivity increased to 173 ± 10 W·m−1·K−1 in both directions. The excerpt does not provide conductivity values as a function of temperature, laser-flash results, or results for direct aging. It also does not quantify separately how stress relief, T6, direct aging, and annealing affect conductivity beyond the cited 300 °C treatment result.

Abstract:
In this study, 27SiMn was selected as a substrate, and the powder was a self-made iron-based alloy. Further, the thermophysical properties of the material were predicted by the CALPHAD phase diagram algorithm. In order to verify the accuracy of the numerical model, 10 sets of experiments were set up. The agreement between the results from the model calculations and the experimental results was 92%. Through the study of energy distribution in the laser cladding process, it was found that about 10% of the laser energy was used to heat the substrate to form a melt pool, and at least 53% of the energy was radiated into the environment. Finally, the effects of the temperature gradient and solidification rate on the microstructure of the cladding layer were explored. The numerical simulation results are helpful in predicting the solidification rate, temperature distribution and microstructure of the melt pool, thereby reducing the cost of testing as well as the time for the experimental method of trial–error.

Abstract:
The low hardness and insufficient wear resistance of aluminum and its alloys restrict their broader application in various fields. The application of surface protective coatings can effectively enhance the hardness and wear resistance of aluminum and its alloys. This article provides a comprehensive review of the recent research progress of wear-resistant coatings fabricated on aluminum and its alloys. The relevant achievements in the recent research works of preparing wear-resistant coatings by one-step methods (such as anodic oxidation, micro-arc oxidation, cold spraying, plasma spraying, and electrodeposition) and two-step methods (anodic oxidation and physical vapor deposition, micro-arc oxidation and sealing, magnetron sputtering, and plasma nitriding) are mainly introduced. The working principles of each coating preparation method, along with their impacts on the microstructure and tribological performance of the coatings, were systematically examined. Additionally, a comparative analysis was conducted to evaluate the advantages and disadvantages of each coating preparation method.

Antonia P. Betzou, Michael Auinger, and Prakash Srirangam. Effect of melt superheat and shear rate on viscosity of aluminium–silicon alloys. Metallurgical and Materials Transactions B, 56:4148-4154, Jun 2025. URL: https://doi.org/10.1007/s11663-025-03626-4, doi:10.1007/s11663-025-03626-4. This article has 2 citations.

The excerpt establishes that Betzou, Auinger, and Srirangam measured liquid-metal viscosity using a rotational rheometer and investigated its dependence on melt superheat and shear rate. The studied compositions were Al–7 wt pct Si, Al–20 wt pct Si, and Al–7 wt pct Si–2 wt pct Fe. The measurements were fitted with an Arrhenius model, but the excerpt does not provide the resulting Arrhenius pre-exponential factors, activation energies, or explicit temperature-dependent viscosity equations. It reports that pure aluminum viscosity values measured in the study ranged from 1.4 to 0.3 Pa s, without specifying the corresponding temperatures in the supplied pages. All tested alloys displayed shear-thinning behavior: viscosity decreased as shear rate increased and reached a steady state above a certain shear limit. The introduction also notes that viscosity values in the literature can differ substantially, by up to 400%, because of measurement technique, alloy purity, inclusions, precipitates, oxidation, intermetallic formation, and melt structure. No numerical dynamic-viscosity correlation for liquid aluminum or Al–Si alloys as a function of temperature, and no Assael et al. recommended reference correlation values, appear in this excerpt; those data would need to be obtained from later sections or the cited literature.

Abstract:
<jats:p>The sustainable production of energy without environmental footprints is a challenge of paramount importance to satisfy the ever-increasing global demand and to promote economic and social growth through a greener perspective. Such awareness has significantly stimulated worldwide efforts aimed at exploring various energy paths and sources, in compliance with the ever more stringent environmental regulations. Research advancements in these fields are directly dependent on the design, fabrication, and implementation of tailored multi-materials for efficient energy production and harvesting and storage devices. Herein, we aim at providing a survey on the ongoing research activities related to various aspects of functional materials for energy production, conversion, and storage. In particular, we present the opportunities and the main open challenges related to multifunctional materials spanning from carbon-based nanostructures for chemical energy conversion, ferroelectric ceramics for energy harvesting, and phase change materials for thermal energy storage to metallic materials for hydrogen technologies, heat exchangers for wind energy, and amphiphobic coatings for the protection of solar panels. The relevance of designing tailored materials for power generation is also presented. Finally, the importance of applying life cycle assessment to materials is emphasized through the case study of AlTiN thin films.</jats:p>

Abstract:
The synergistic effect between strontium (Sr) and melt quenching on the solidified microstructure of hypereutectic Al-Si alloys was investigated by optical and scanning electron microscopy. The results indicate that melt quenching can suppress the growth of primary Si particles in the solidified structure of the hypereutectic Al-Si alloy, resulting in a significant decrease of in the average size of primary Si particles in Al-(18~22)Si alloys from 30.35~66.31 μm to 15.13~34.63 μm. The synergistic effect between Sr and melt quenching can further inhibit the precipitation of primary Si particles in the Al-18Si alloy. After the addition of Sr to Al-18Si alloy and undergoing melt quenching, the area fraction of primary Si clearly decreases. When the added amount of Sr increases from 0.1 wt.% to 0.5 wt.%, the area fraction of primary Si decreases from 1.13% to 0.16%. With 0.5 wt.% Sr in the tested alloy, the inhibiting effect on primary Si precipitation was significantly improved. Research has shown that the cooling rate has a significant impact on the solidified structure of the melt-quenched Al-18Si-0.5Sr alloy. There exists no primary Si in solidified structures on the area of 1/8R and 1/4R from the surface of the round bar sample, but the area fraction of primary Si increases, respectively, to 1.97% and 12.48% on the area of 1/2R and R from the surface. The higher the cooling rate, the higher the inhibitory effect on the primary Si precipitation in the Al-18Si-0.5Sr alloy.

Abstract:
<jats:p>The chemical modification of Al–20Si alloy in the case of incorporation of rare earth cerium (Ce) is investigated in this study, focusing on the resulting microstructure evolution and changes in mechanical properties and hardness before and after cerium modification. The microstructure of the cerium-modified alloy is composed of the aluminum matrix, eutectic silicon, and primary silicon phases, as well as the Al2Si2Ce phase, a cerium-containing solid solution, and the α-Al11Ce3 phase. It is worth noting that this study reports for the first time an unusual phenomenon in which the addition of cerium raises tensile strength of the alloy while concurrently decreasing its surface hardness. The increase in tensile strength is mainly ascribed to the refinement of primary silicon. On the contrary, the reduction of hardness is explained by the competition between Ce-induced toughening and solid solution strengthening, as well as the generation of the relatively soft α-Al11Ce3 phase. Mechanical properties at room temperature show that the greatest tensile strength of 153 ± 7 MPa is reached at a cerium concentration of 0.7 wt.%, while the corresponding elongation of the mechanical specimen is 1.36 ± 0.287. The fracture mechanism changes from cleavage fracture in the unmodified alloy to ductile fracture after Ce addition.</jats:p>

Abstract:
An optimisation model for small datasets was applied to thixocasted/compocasted composites and hybrid composites with hypereutectic Al-18Si base alloys. Composites were produced with the addition of Al2O3 (36 µm/25 nm) or SiC (40 µm) particles. Based on the design of experiment, tribological tests were performed on the tribometer with block-on-disc contact geometry for normal loads of 100 and 200 N, a sliding speed of 0.5 m/s, and a sliding distance of 1000 m. For the prediction of the tribological behaviour of composites, artificial neural networks (ANNs) were used. Three inputs were considered for ANN training: type of reinforcement (base alloy, Al2O3 and SiC), amount of Al2O3 nano-reinforcement (0 and 0.5 wt.%), and load (100 and 200 N). Various ANNs were applied, and the best ANN for wear rate (WR), with an overall regression coefficient of 0.99484, was a network with architecture 3-15-1 and a logsig (logarithmic sigmoid) transfer function. For coefficient of friction (CoF), the best ANN was the one with architecture 3-6-1 and a tansig (hyperbolic tangent sigmoid) transfer function and had an overall regression coefficient of 0.93096. To investigate the potential of ANN for the prediction of two outputs simultaneously, an ANN was trained, and the best results were from network 3-5-2 with a logsig transfer function and overall regression coefficient of 0.99776, but the predicted values for CoF in this case did not show good correlation with experimental results. After the selection of the best ANNs, the Taguchi grey multi-response optimisation of WR and CoF was performed for the same combination of factors as the ANNs. For optimal WR and CoF, the combination of factors was as follows: composite with 3 wt.% Al2O3 micro-reinforcement, 0.5 wt.% Al2O3 nano-reinforcement, and a load of 100 N. The results show that developed ANN, the Taguchi method, and the Taguchi grey method can, with high reliability, be used for the optimisation of wear rate and coefficient of friction of hypereutectic Al-Si composites. Microstructural investigations of worn surfaces were performed, and the wear mechanism for all tested materials was light abrasion and adhesion. The findings from this research can contribute to the future development of hypereutectic Al-Si composites.

Abstract:
This research aimed to investigate the effects of bismuth (Bi) and phosphorus (P) addition on the microstructure and roughness of a B390 hypereutectic Al-Si alloy. Microstructural variation of as-cast alloys showed that P is an effective refiner of primary Si and its distribution, while Bi has the opposite effect. The liquidus temperature increased with greater amounts of P, resulting in a wider solidification range. The solidus temperature increased with Bi content, resulting in a shortened solidification range. The benefit of Bi on eutectic silicon was through changing its morphology from fibrous to lamellar structures. It was observed that both primary Si and eutectic Si were modified when both P and Bi were added to the alloys. For effective refinement, the size of primary Si can be reduced by 50.6% and, the P content should not be less than 0.1 wt% with a Bi content of 0.5–1.0 wt%. Furthermore, an intermetallic phase size reduction also occurs. P addition results in a significant (5.85%) increase in hardness. Adding Bi (up to 1.0 wt%) together with P (up to 0.1 wt%) did not reduce the effect of P on the hardness of the modified alloys. The most effective reduction in roughness achieved during cutting at both low and high speeds was 26.5% and 57.7%, respectively, from modifying the B390 alloy using 0.1 wt%P with 1.0 wt%Bi.

Abstract:
An hypereutectic Al–18Si alloy was modified via an Al–3B master alloy. The effect of the added Al–3B and the modification temperature on the microstructure, tensile fracture morphologies, and mechanical properties of the alloy were investigated using an optical microscope, Image–Pro Plus 6.0, a scanning electron microscope, and a universal testing machine. The results show that the size of the primary Si and its fraction decreased at first, and then increased as an additional amount of Al–3B was added. When the added Al–3B reached 0.2 wt %, the fraction of the primary Si in the Al–18Si alloy decreased with an increase in temperature. Compared with the unmodified Al–18Si alloy, the tensile strength and elongation of the alloy modified at 850 °C with 0.2 wt % Al–3B increased by 25% and 81%, respectively. The tensile fracture of the modified Al–18Si alloy exhibited partial ductile fracture characteristics, but there were more areas with ductile characteristics compared with that of the unmodified Al–18Si alloy.

Abstract:
Among the thermophysical properties, the surface / interfacial tension, viscosity and density / molar volume of liquid alloys are the key properties for the modelling of microstructural evolution during solidification. Therefore, only reliable input data can yield accurate predictions preventing the error propagation in numerical simulations of solidification related processes. Due to experimental difficulties related to reactivity of metallic melts at high temperatures, the measured data are often unreliable or even lacking. The application of containerless processing techniques either leads to a significant improvement of the accuracy or makes the measurement possible at all. On the other side, accurate model predicted property values could be used to compensate the missing data; otherwise, the experimental data are useful for the validation of theoretical models. The choice of models is particularly important for the surface, transport and structural properties of liquid alloys representing the two limiting cases of mixing, i.e. ordered and phase separating alloy systems. To this aim, the thermophysical properties of the Fe-Si and Cu-Pb systems were analysed and the connections with the peculiarities of their mixing behaviours are highlighted.

## pqac-00000027

From text 'fulkerson1968thermalconductivityelectrical pages 10-11'.

W. Fulkerson, J. P. Moore, R. K. Williams, R. S. Graves, and D. L. McElroy. Thermal conductivity, electrical resistivity, and seebeck coefficient of silicon from 100 to 1300°k. Physical Review, 167:765-782, Mar 1968. URL: https://doi.org/10.1103/physrev.167.765, doi:10.1103/physrev.167.765. This article has 325 citations.

This excerpt provides information about fitting the thermal resistivity of silicon, rather than a complete tabulation of thermal conductivity values from 300 to 1300 K. The authors state that the thermal-resistivity data are represented closely by linear relations over 130–1050 K, with separate behavior below and above approximately 670 K. The reported average slopes are 2.946×10^? cm/W below 670 K and 4.287×10^? cm/W above 670 K, corresponding to an increase of about 45%; the OCR has lost the exponent formatting and the table containing the fitted intercepts and slopes is incomplete. The excerpt also notes that the thermal conductivity bends down at high temperatures, attributed to an electronic contribution, and that data from different thermocouple types showed the same effect. Consequently, this passage alone does not provide sufficient explicit numerical values in W/m·K at selected temperatures between 300 and 1300 K. To calculate or tabulate those values, the complete Table V (including A and B for the thermal-resistivity relation), the correct units/exponents, and the conversion from resistivity to conductivity would be needed.

## pqac-00000028

From text 'fulkerson1968thermalconductivityelectrical pages 1-2'.

W. Fulkerson, J. P. Moore, R. K. Williams, R. S. Graves, and D. L. McElroy. Thermal conductivity, electrical resistivity, and seebeck coefficient of silicon from 100 to 1300°k. Physical Review, 167:765-782, Mar 1968. URL: https://doi.org/10.1103/physrev.167.765, doi:10.1103/physrev.167.765. This article has 325 citations.

The excerpt identifies Fulkerson et al.’s 1968 paper as reporting thermal-conductivity measurements for high-purity silicon over 90–1328 K, which covers the requested 300–1300 K range. Measurements above 387 K used an absolute radial heat-flow method, while intermediate measurements from 300–400 K were also obtained for polycrystalline silicon using a comparative longitudinal heat-flow apparatus. The reported estimated uncertainties were approximately ±2% above 387 K, ±1.2% for the low-temperature longitudinal method, and ±4% for the comparative 300–400 K measurements. Qualitatively, the paper states that thermal conductivity decreases with increasing temperature, with an abrupt change in the slope of thermal resistivity near 670 K. At high temperatures, the authors support the higher-temperature results of Glassbrenner and Slack, in which conductivity continues to decrease, though more slowly than at lower temperatures. However, this excerpt contains no numerical thermal-conductivity table, graph values, or specific conductivity values in W/m-K. Therefore, exact values at selected temperatures between 300 and 1300 K cannot be extracted from the supplied pages; the paper’s subsequent data tables or figures would be needed.

## pqac-00000029

From text 'fulkerson1968thermalconductivityelectrical pages 14-15'.

W. Fulkerson, J. P. Moore, R. K. Williams, R. S. Graves, and D. L. McElroy. Thermal conductivity, electrical resistivity, and seebeck coefficient of silicon from 100 to 1300°k. Physical Review, 167:765-782, Mar 1968. URL: https://doi.org/10.1103/physrev.167.765, doi:10.1103/physrev.167.765. This article has 325 citations.

The excerpt discusses the thermal-conductivity analysis of silicon, particularly the separation of lattice and electronic contributions. It states that the electronic contribution, k_e, is less than 1% of the total thermal conductivity below approximately 900 K, but becomes increasingly important at higher temperatures. The authors therefore initially neglect direct radiation transmission and the electronic contribution in interpreting the lattice thermal-resistance data, while noting that radiation effects could be on the order of 2% below 600 K. A plotted figure is identified as showing silicon lattice thermal resistivity, apparently over a temperature range extending from roughly 200 to 1400 K, which includes the requested 300–1300 K interval. However, the excerpt does not provide a readable numerical table or sufficiently clear graph values for converting the plotted resistivity into thermal conductivity in W/m-K at specific temperatures. It also notes that the electronic-contribution calculation is based on a simplified two-parabolic-band model and may be affected by silicon’s more complex electronic band structure. Thus, this passage supports qualitative interpretation of temperature-dependent conductivity and measurement corrections, but additional readable figure data or tabulated values from the full article would be needed for reliable values at 300, 400, 500 K, and so forth through 1300 K.

Abstract:
A brief review of measurement techniques and theoretical studies on the surface tension alloy and mixture has been presented in the present study. It is clear that the experimental determination of thermodynamic and thermophysical properties of both solid and especially liquid alloys at high temperature cases is frequently difficult technologically. In addition to this, a lack of experimental data concerning thermophysical properties of Ag-Au, Au-Cu, and Ag-Cu sub-binary systems is obvious. The theoretical thermophysical data of the Ag-Au-Cu ternary alloy systems are very scarce in the literature. Thus, the surface tensions of the alloys just mentioned above for cross sections z = xAg/xAu = 1/3, 1/1, 3/1, 2/5, and 5/2, respectively, and their sub-binary systems are much simply calculated from the surface tensions of the Ag-Au, Au-Cu, and Ag-Cu sub-binary systems by using geometric models, such as Muggianu, Kohler, Toop, and GSM (Chou’s general solution model) and Butler’s equation. The predicted results in the present study show rather an agreement with the experimental results of the alloys. Therefore, it is inferred that the obtained surface tension curves for the Ag-Au-Cu ternary alloy at 1381 K are reasonable with especially those calculated from the Toop model.

Arad Azizi, Fatemeh Hejripour, Jacob A. Goodman, Piyush A. Kulkarni, Xiaobo Chen, Guangwen Zhou, and Scott N. Schiffres. Process-dependent anisotropic thermal conductivity of laser powder bed fusion alsi10mg: impact of microstructure and aluminum-silicon interfaces. Rapid Prototyping Journal, 29:1109-1120, Feb 2023. URL: https://doi.org/10.1108/rpj-09-2022-0290, doi:10.1108/rpj-09-2022-0290. This article has 24 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

This excerpt confirms that the study measured LPBF AlSi10Mg thermal conductivity using flash diffusivity and frequency-domain thermoreflectance (FDTR), and that it examined processing conditions, build orientation, and microstructure. However, the provided pages do not report thermal conductivity as a function of temperature over the elevated-temperature range of 100–500°C, nor do they provide specific numerical conductivity values at individual temperatures within that range. The only numerical conductivity results visible here are process-dependent peak values: a maximum through-plane conductivity of approximately 1366 W/m-K at an energy density of 59 J/mm³ and a peak in-plane conductivity of approximately 1176 W/m-K at 50 J/mm³. The abstract attributes conductivity changes primarily to grain size and the number of Al-Si interfaces, with larger columnar grain colonies having higher conductivity. To answer the temperature-specific question, the full paper’s experimental results, figures, or tables—particularly the flash-diffusivity temperature measurements—would be required. The excerpt alone cannot establish numerical values at 100°C, 200°C, 300°C, 400°C, or 500°C.

## pqac-00000038

From text 'azizi2023processdependentanisotropicthermal pages 2-3'.

Arad Azizi, Fatemeh Hejripour, Jacob A. Goodman, Piyush A. Kulkarni, Xiaobo Chen, Guangwen Zhou, and Scott N. Schiffres. Process-dependent anisotropic thermal conductivity of laser powder bed fusion alsi10mg: impact of microstructure and aluminum-silicon interfaces. Rapid Prototyping Journal, 29:1109-1120, Feb 2023. URL: https://doi.org/10.1108/rpj-09-2022-0290, doi:10.1108/rpj-09-2022-0290. This article has 24 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt provides methodological and comparative information but does not report the specific thermal-conductivity values of LPBF AlSi10Mg at 100, 200, 300, 400, or 500°C. It states that earlier studies measured thermal conductivity as a function of temperature and heat treatment, and that heat-treated material showed 18–41% higher thermal conductivity than the untreated condition. It also reports that no substantial difference was observed among post-heat-treated thermal conductivities for annealing temperatures between 300 and 500°C; these are annealing conditions, not necessarily measurement temperatures. For the present study, thermal diffusivity was measured using flash diffusivity on polished 8 × 8 × 3.5 mm samples coated with graphite to enhance flash absorption. Thermal conductivity values would require the temperature-dependent results or cited source studies not included in this excerpt. The passage also explains that as-built AlSi10Mg has lower conductivity than pure aluminum because Si and Mg create phonon- and electron-scattering sites, while heat treatment transforms intergranular silicon films into spherical precipitates, reducing thermal interfaces and improving conductivity.

Surface Tension of Molten Al–Si Alloys Measured
by Electromagnetic Levitation: Comparison with Ideal‑
and Subregular‑Solution Calculations

Yusaku Seimiya1,2     · Haruto Yoneyama1 · Shumpei Ozawa1 


Received: 14 August 2026 / Accepted: 12 September 2026 / Published online: 9 October 2026
© The Author(s) 2026


Abstract
Surface tension data for molten Al–Si alloys are important for modeling high-tem-
perature melt-processing phenomena, but the surface tension values in the literature
show considerable scatter, particularly with respect to their composition depend-
ence. In this study, surface tension measurements were conducted for pure liquid
Al, pure liquid Si, and molten Al–Si alloys containing 5–80 at % Si using the oscil-
lating drop method with electromagnetic levitation. Oxide-affected heating curves
were excluded from the pyrometer calibration, and only oscillation data for which
no oxide film was observed on the droplet surface were analyzed. For all exam-
ined compositions, the measured surface tension decreased linearly with increasing
temperature. Near 1700 K, the surface tension decreased monotonically and nearly
linearly with increasing Si concentration, and previously reported nonlinear behav-
iors, such as relatively high values in the Al-rich region and an increase toward the
Si-rich side, were not observed. Uncertainty analysis confirmed that the nearly lin-
ear composition dependence was not due to measurement uncertainty. Butler equa-
tion calculations were performed using the pure-component surface tension values
obtained in this study. The ideal-solution approximation reproduced the measured
composition dependence and temperature coefficients more consistently than the
subregular-solution calculation using the evaluated excess Gibbs energies. These
results indicate that thermodynamic nonideality makes only a limited contribution to
the surface tension behavior of molten Al–Si alloys under the present experimental
conditions.

Keywords  Al–Si alloys · Butler equation · Electromagnetic levitation · Ideal-
solution approximation · Surface tension


* Yusaku Seimiya
    [email redacted]
1   Department of Materials Science and Engineering, Chiba Institute of Technology, 2‑17‑1
    Tsudanuma, Narashino, Chiba 275‑0016, Japan
2   Department of Physics, Gakushuin University, 1‑5‑1 Mejiro, Toshima, Tokyo 171‑8588, Japan

1  Introduction

Al–Si alloys are widely used in high-temperature melt-processing applications
such as casting and brazing. In these processes, surface tension plays an important
role in melt flow, capillary-driven infiltration, mold filling, joint formation, and
defect formation. Reliable data on the temperature and composition dependences
of surface tension are therefore essential for quantitative modeling and numerical
simulation of such processes. Surface tension and related interfacial properties of
Al–Si and Al–Si-based alloys have been investigated in previous studies [1–6].
However, even for binary Al–Si alloys, the surface tension data reported in the
literature are not fully consistent [1, 2, 6]. Some studies have reported a nearly
monotonic decrease in surface tension with increasing Si concentration, whereas
others have reported relatively high values in the Al-rich region and an increase
in the surface tension toward the Si-rich side. Furthermore, even the data reported
for pure liquid Al and pure liquid Si show considerable scatter [6–18]. The differ-
ences in the experimental surface tension values and trends may be related to dif-
ferences in the experimental conditions, data analysis procedures, sample purity,
contamination from supporting materials, and oxygen-related effects at the melt
surface. In particular, because liquid Al is highly susceptible to oxidation, surface
oxidation or oxide film formation may affect the droplet shape and surface condi-
tions, thereby contributing to the scatter in the reported data. However, the rela-
tively high surface tension values reported in the Al-rich region and the increase
in the surface tension toward the Si-rich side cannot be readily explained by sim-
ple oxygen adsorption alone because surface-active oxygen is generally expected
to reduce, rather than increase, the surface tension of molten metals and alloys.
In addition to these experimental factors, thermodynamic nonideality may also
influence the composition dependence of the surface tension through changes in
the surface composition.
   Therefore, a comparison between the measured surface tension and thermo-
dynamic calculations can be used to clarify whether the reported nonlinear com-
position dependences of surface tension reflect the thermodynamic behavior of
molten Al–Si alloys or arise from experimental factors. However, the role played
by thermodynamic nonideality in the surface tension of molten Al–Si alloys has
not been elucidated to date.
   In this study, surface tension measurements were conducted for pure liquid Al,
pure liquid Si, and molten Al–Si alloys using the oscillating drop method with
electromagnetic levitation (EML). This method enables container-free measure-
ments and minimizes contamination from the supporting materials. To elucidate
the composition dependence of the surface tension in the Al–Si system and evalu-
ate the role of thermodynamic nonideality, the measured values were compared
with Butler equation calculations using the pure-component surface tensions
obtained in this study. Calculations were performed using both the evaluated
excess Gibbs energies and the ideal-solution approximation to examine how ther-
modynamic nonideality affects the surface tension of molten Al–Si alloys.International Journal of Thermophysics (2026) 47:170                               Page 3 of 14  170

2  Experimental Procedure

High-purity aluminum (> 99.99 mass %) and silicon (electrical resistivity: 1.2 × ­10–2
Ω·cm) were used as starting materials. Small pieces of Al and Si were cut and ultra-
sonically cleaned in a hydrofluoric-nitric acid solution (HF:HNO3 = 1:3 by volume)
to remove surface oxides and then rinsed with acetone. For alloy measurements, one
piece each of Al and Si was placed on a quartz holder in the EML chamber.
  A high-purity Ar–He gas mixture with an oxygen partial pressure, PO2 , of ­10−2 Pa
was continuously supplied to the chamber at a flow rate of 2 L·min−1. First, the Al
sample was electromagnetically levitated and melted by applying a high-frequency
current to the coil. The Si sample was then brought into contact with the levitated
Al droplet, and the two pieces were levitated together. The Si sample subsequently
melted into the Al melt to form a single alloy droplet under container-free condi-
tions. To levitate and melt pure Si without molten Al, the Si sample was first pre-
heated by laser irradiation to increase its electrical conductivity. Once sufficiently
preheated,  it was electromagnetically levitated and melted by induction heating.
Nominal alloy compositions were calculated from the initial masses of Al and Si.
The maximum mass loss during the measurements was less than 0.25 % of the initial
sample mass, corresponding to less than 1 mg for the 400 mg sample. Assuming that
the entire mass loss originated from the evaporation of either Al or Si, the resulting
change in the alloy composition was estimated to be less than 0.3 at % for all alloy
compositions examined in this study. This value is much smaller than the compo-
sition intervals of the measurements. Therefore, the effect of the mass loss on the
alloy composition was considered to be negligible.
  The droplet temperature was measured using a monochromatic pyrometer with
a wavelength range of λ = 1.45–1.6 μm and controlled by adjusting the Ar/He gas
flow ratio. For the emissivity calibration, the droplet was temporarily solidified by
switching the atmosphere from the Ar–He gas mixture to He gas at an increased
flow rate of 10 L·min−1, followed by reheating. During reheating, a distinct inflec-
tion point corresponding to the completion of melting was observed in the pyrometer
signal. The emissivity setting of the pyrometer was adjusted such that the apparent
temperature at this inflection point matched the equilibrium liquidus temperature,
TL , of each Al–Si alloy. Only the heating curves for which no oxide was observed
within the pyrometer measurement spot in the high-speed video (HSV) images were
used for this calibration. This is because the higher emissivity of the oxide com-
pared to the molten alloy gives rise to an overestimation of the apparent temperature
when the oxide is present within the pyrometer spot.

Abstract:
In industrial practice, various methods of external influences on metal melts are used. For example, vibration processing, exposure to ultrasound, and other physical fields. The main purpose of such influences is purposeful grinding of the metal structure, which contributes to the improvement of mechanical characteristics. The article presents an overview of research on pulse processing of ferrous and non-ferrous melts: processing with pulsed current, electromagnetic pulses and pulsed magnetic fields. The results of the analysis showed that, despite the different methods and devices used for these treatments, their effect on the structure and properties of the cast metal is generally the same. The main effect is observed in the refinement of the macro and microstructure and a simultaneous increase in the strength properties and plasticity. The intensity of the observed effects depends on the characteristics of the equipment used to create the pulses. The main characteristics are: pulse duration, pulse frequency, current amplitude, and power.

Abstract:
With the rapid expansion of battery-powered electric vehicles (BEVs) in the automotive industry, research interest in lightweight Al alloys as well as their casting processes and applications has increased considerably. The substitution of castable aluminum alloys with superior strengths and electrical conductivity for copper reduces the weight and size of electric induction motors, and improves the energy efficiency and driving range of the BEVs. The present article was intended to give a general introduction into the common cast Al aluminum alloys and their relevant processes, as well as to motivate the development of high strength and conductive Al alloys for the practical realization of Al applications in the motors of the BEVs. A number of cast alloy systems containing Cu, Si, Ni, Mg, Fe, and Ti were evaluated, in comparison to nanostructured wrought Al alloys. The conventional casting processes suitable for Al alloys, high pressure die casting, squeeze casting, and sand casting were described. Strengthening mechanisms including solid solution strengthening, precipitation strengthening, dislocation accumulation strengthening, and grain boundary strengthening were presented. The phenomenon of electrical conduction for Al alloys was outlined. The mechanical properties and electrical properties of the recently developed Al alloys for casting and deformation processes were comprehensively listed and critically reviewed in association with microstructural characteristics.
