## pqac-00000027

From text 'fulkerson1968thermalconductivityelectrical pages 10-11'.

W. Fulkerson, J. P. Moore, R. K. Williams, R. S. Graves, and D. L. McElroy. Thermal conductivity, electrical resistivity, and seebeck coefficient of silicon from 100 to 1300°k. Physical Review, 167:765-782, Mar 1968. URL: https://doi.org/10.1103/physrev.167.765, doi:10.1103/physrev.167.765. This article has 325 citations.

This excerpt provides information about fitting the thermal resistivity of silicon, rather than a complete tabulation of thermal conductivity values from 300 to 1300 K. The authors state that the thermal-resistivity data are represented closely by linear relations over 130–1050 K, with separate behavior below and above approximately 670 K. The reported average slopes are 2.946×10^? cm/W below 670 K and 4.287×10^? cm/W above 670 K, corresponding to an increase of about 45%; the OCR has lost the exponent formatting and the table containing the fitted intercepts and slopes is incomplete. The excerpt also notes that the thermal conductivity bends down at high temperatures, attributed to an electronic contribution, and that data from different thermocouple types showed the same effect. Consequently, this passage alone does not provide sufficient explicit numerical values in W/m·K at selected temperatures between 300 and 1300 K. To calculate or tabulate those values, the complete Table V (including A and B for the thermal-resistivity relation), the correct units/exponents, and the conversion from resistivity to conductivity would be needed.


---

## pqac-00000028

From text 'fulkerson1968thermalconductivityelectrical pages 1-2'.

W. Fulkerson, J. P. Moore, R. K. Williams, R. S. Graves, and D. L. McElroy. Thermal conductivity, electrical resistivity, and seebeck coefficient of silicon from 100 to 1300°k. Physical Review, 167:765-782, Mar 1968. URL: https://doi.org/10.1103/physrev.167.765, doi:10.1103/physrev.167.765. This article has 325 citations.

The excerpt identifies Fulkerson et al.’s 1968 paper as reporting thermal-conductivity measurements for high-purity silicon over 90–1328 K, which covers the requested 300–1300 K range. Measurements above 387 K used an absolute radial heat-flow method, while intermediate measurements from 300–400 K were also obtained for polycrystalline silicon using a comparative longitudinal heat-flow apparatus. The reported estimated uncertainties were approximately ±2% above 387 K, ±1.2% for the low-temperature longitudinal method, and ±4% for the comparative 300–400 K measurements. Qualitatively, the paper states that thermal conductivity decreases with increasing temperature, with an abrupt change in the slope of thermal resistivity near 670 K. At high temperatures, the authors support the higher-temperature results of Glassbrenner and Slack, in which conductivity continues to decrease, though more slowly than at lower temperatures. However, this excerpt contains no numerical thermal-conductivity table, graph values, or specific conductivity values in W/m-K. Therefore, exact values at selected temperatures between 300 and 1300 K cannot be extracted from the supplied pages; the paper’s subsequent data tables or figures would be needed.


---

## pqac-00000029

From text 'fulkerson1968thermalconductivityelectrical pages 14-15'.

W. Fulkerson, J. P. Moore, R. K. Williams, R. S. Graves, and D. L. McElroy. Thermal conductivity, electrical resistivity, and seebeck coefficient of silicon from 100 to 1300°k. Physical Review, 167:765-782, Mar 1968. URL: https://doi.org/10.1103/physrev.167.765, doi:10.1103/physrev.167.765. This article has 325 citations.

The excerpt discusses the thermal-conductivity analysis of silicon, particularly the separation of lattice and electronic contributions. It states that the electronic contribution, k_e, is less than 1% of the total thermal conductivity below approximately 900 K, but becomes increasingly important at higher temperatures. The authors therefore initially neglect direct radiation transmission and the electronic contribution in interpreting the lattice thermal-resistance data, while noting that radiation effects could be on the order of 2% below 600 K. A plotted figure is identified as showing silicon lattice thermal resistivity, apparently over a temperature range extending from roughly 200 to 1400 K, which includes the requested 300–1300 K interval. However, the excerpt does not provide a readable numerical table or sufficiently clear graph values for converting the plotted resistivity into thermal conductivity in W/m-K at specific temperatures. It also notes that the electronic-contribution calculation is based on a simplified two-parabolic-band model and may be affected by silicon’s more complex electronic band structure. Thus, this passage supports qualitative interpretation of temperature-dependent conductivity and measurement corrections, but additional readable figure data or tabulated values from the full article would be needed for reliable values at 300, 400, 500 K, and so forth through 1300 K.

Abstract:
A brief review of measurement techniques and theoretical studies on the surface tension alloy and mixture has been presented in the present study. It is clear that the experimental determination of thermodynamic and thermophysical properties of both solid and especially liquid alloys at high temperature cases is frequently difficult technologically. In addition to this, a lack of experimental data concerning thermophysical properties of Ag-Au, Au-Cu, and Ag-Cu sub-binary systems is obvious. The theoretical thermophysical data of the Ag-Au-Cu ternary alloy systems are very scarce in the literature. Thus, the surface tensions of the alloys just mentioned above for cross sections z = xAg/xAu = 1/3, 1/1, 3/1, 2/5, and 5/2, respectively, and their sub-binary systems are much simply calculated from the surface tensions of the Ag-Au, Au-Cu, and Ag-Cu sub-binary systems by using geometric models, such as Muggianu, Kohler, Toop, and GSM (Chou’s general solution model) and Butler’s equation. The predicted results in the present study show rather an agreement with the experimental results of the alloys. Therefore, it is inferred that the obtained surface tension curves for the Ag-Au-Cu ternary alloy at 1381 K are reasonable with especially those calculated from the Toop model.

International Journal of Thermophysics (2026) 47:170
https://doi.org/10.1007/s10765-026-03847-y



Surface Tension of Molten Al–Si Alloys Measured
by Electromagnetic Levitation: Comparison with Ideal‑
and Subregular‑Solution Calculations

Yusaku Seimiya1,2     · Haruto Yoneyama1 · Shumpei Ozawa1 


Received: 14 August 2026 / Accepted: 12 September 2026 / Published online: 9 October 2026
© The Author(s) 2026


Abstract
Surface tension data for molten Al–Si alloys are important for modeling high-tem-
perature melt-processing phenomena, but the surface tension values in the literature
show considerable scatter, particularly with respect to their composition depend-
ence. In this study, surface tension measurements were conducted for pure liquid
Al, pure liquid Si, and molten Al–Si alloys containing 5–80 at % Si using the oscil-
lating drop method with electromagnetic levitation. Oxide-affected heating curves
were excluded from the pyrometer calibration, and only oscillation data for which
no oxide film was observed on the droplet surface were analyzed. For all exam-
ined compositions, the measured surface tension decreased linearly with increasing
temperature. Near 1700 K, the surface tension decreased monotonically and nearly
linearly with increasing Si concentration, and previously reported nonlinear behav-
iors, such as relatively high values in the Al-rich region and an increase toward the
Si-rich side, were not observed. Uncertainty analysis confirmed that the nearly lin-
ear composition dependence was not due to measurement uncertainty. Butler equa-
tion calculations were performed using the pure-component surface tension values
obtained in this study. The ideal-solution approximation reproduced the measured
composition dependence and temperature coefficients more consistently than the
subregular-solution calculation using the evaluated excess Gibbs energies. These
results indicate that thermodynamic nonideality makes only a limited contribution to
the surface tension behavior of molten Al–Si alloys under the present experimental
conditions.

Keywords  Al–Si alloys · Butler equation · Electromagnetic levitation · Ideal-
solution approximation · Surface tension


* Yusaku Seimiya
    [email redacted]
1   Department of Materials Science and Engineering, Chiba Institute of Technology, 2‑17‑1
    Tsudanuma, Narashino, Chiba 275‑0016, Japan
2   Department of Physics, Gakushuin University, 1‑5‑1 Mejiro, Toshima, Tokyo 171‑8588, Japan

1  Introduction

Al–Si alloys are widely used in high-temperature melt-processing applications
such as casting and brazing. In these processes, surface tension plays an important
role in melt flow, capillary-driven infiltration, mold filling, joint formation, and
defect formation. Reliable data on the temperature and composition dependences
of surface tension are therefore essential for quantitative modeling and numerical
simulation of such processes. Surface tension and related interfacial properties of
Al–Si and Al–Si-based alloys have been investigated in previous studies [1–6].
However, even for binary Al–Si alloys, the surface tension data reported in the
literature are not fully consistent [1, 2, 6]. Some studies have reported a nearly
monotonic decrease in surface tension with increasing Si concentration, whereas
others have reported relatively high values in the Al-rich region and an increase
in the surface tension toward the Si-rich side. Furthermore, even the data reported
for pure liquid Al and pure liquid Si show considerable scatter [6–18]. The differ-
ences in the experimental surface tension values and trends may be related to dif-
ferences in the experimental conditions, data analysis procedures, sample purity,
contamination from supporting materials, and oxygen-related effects at the melt
surface. In particular, because liquid Al is highly susceptible to oxidation, surface
oxidation or oxide film formation may affect the droplet shape and surface condi-
tions, thereby contributing to the scatter in the reported data. However, the rela-
tively high surface tension values reported in the Al-rich region and the increase
in the surface tension toward the Si-rich side cannot be readily explained by sim-
ple oxygen adsorption alone because surface-active oxygen is generally expected
to reduce, rather than increase, the surface tension of molten metals and alloys.
In addition to these experimental factors, thermodynamic nonideality may also
influence the composition dependence of the surface tension through changes in
the surface composition.
   Therefore, a comparison between the measured surface tension and thermo-
dynamic calculations can be used to clarify whether the reported nonlinear com-
position dependences of surface tension reflect the thermodynamic behavior of
molten Al–Si alloys or arise from experimental factors. However, the role played
by thermodynamic nonideality in the surface tension of molten Al–Si alloys has
not been elucidated to date.
   In this study, surface tension measurements were conducted for pure liquid Al,
pure liquid Si, and molten Al–Si alloys using the oscillating drop method with
electromagnetic levitation (EML). This method enables container-free measure-
ments and minimizes contamination from the supporting materials. To elucidate
the composition dependence of the surface tension in the Al–Si system and evalu-
ate the role of thermodynamic nonideality, the measured values were compared
with Butler equation calculations using the pure-component surface tensions
obtained in this study. Calculations were performed using both the evaluated
excess Gibbs energies and the ideal-solution approximation to examine how ther-
modynamic nonideality affects the surface tension of molten Al–Si alloys.International Journal of Thermophysics (2026) 47:170                               Page 3 of 14  170

2  Experimental Procedure

High-purity aluminum (> 99.99 mass %) and silicon (electrical resistivity: 1.2 × ­10–2
Ω·cm) were used as starting materials. Small pieces of Al and Si were cut and ultra-
sonically cleaned in a hydrofluoric-nitric acid solution (HF:HNO3 = 1:3 by volume)
to remove surface oxides and then rinsed with acetone. For alloy measurements, one
piece each of Al and Si was placed on a quartz holder in the EML chamber.
  A high-purity Ar–He gas mixture with an oxygen partial pressure, PO2 , of ­10−2 Pa
was continuously supplied to the chamber at a flow rate of 2 L·min−1. First, the Al
sample was electromagnetically levitated and melted by applying a high-frequency
current to the coil. The Si sample was then brought into contact with the levitated
Al droplet, and the two pieces were levitated together. The Si sample subsequently
melted into the Al melt to form a single alloy droplet under container-free condi-
tions. To levitate and melt pure Si without molten Al, the Si sample was first pre-
heated by laser irradiation to increase its electrical conductivity. Once sufficiently
preheated,  it was electromagnetically levitated and melted by induction heating.
Nominal alloy compositions were calculated from the initial masses of Al and Si.
The maximum mass loss during the measurements was less than 0.25 % of the initial
sample mass, corresponding to less than 1 mg for the 400 mg sample. Assuming that
the entire mass loss originated from the evaporation of either Al or Si, the resulting
change in the alloy composition was estimated to be less than 0.3 at % for all alloy
compositions examined in this study. This value is much smaller than the compo-
sition intervals of the measurements. Therefore, the effect of the mass loss on the
alloy composition was considered to be negligible.
  The droplet temperature was measured using a monochromatic pyrometer with
a wavelength range of λ = 1.45–1.6 μm and controlled by adjusting the Ar/He gas
flow ratio. For the emissivity calibration, the droplet was temporarily solidified by
switching the atmosphere from the Ar–He gas mixture to He gas at an increased
flow rate of 10 L·min−1, followed by reheating. During reheating, a distinct inflec-
tion point corresponding to the completion of melting was observed in the pyrometer
signal. The emissivity setting of the pyrometer was adjusted such that the apparent
temperature at this inflection point matched the equilibrium liquidus temperature,
TL , of each Al–Si alloy. Only the heating curves for which no oxide was observed
within the pyrometer measurement spot in the high-speed video (HSV) images were
used for this calibration. This is because the higher emissivity of the oxide com-
pared to the molten alloy gives rise to an overestimation of the apparent temperature
when the oxide is present within the pyrometer spot.

Abstract:
In industrial practice, various methods of external influences on metal melts are used. For example, vibration processing, exposure to ultrasound, and other physical fields. The main purpose of such influences is purposeful grinding of the metal structure, which contributes to the improvement of mechanical characteristics. The article presents an overview of research on pulse processing of ferrous and non-ferrous melts: processing with pulsed current, electromagnetic pulses and pulsed magnetic fields. The results of the analysis showed that, despite the different methods and devices used for these treatments, their effect on the structure and properties of the cast metal is generally the same. The main effect is observed in the refinement of the macro and microstructure and a simultaneous increase in the strength properties and plasticity. The intensity of the observed effects depends on the characteristics of the equipment used to create the pulses. The main characteristics are: pulse duration, pulse frequency, current amplitude, and power.

Abstract:
With the rapid expansion of battery-powered electric vehicles (BEVs) in the automotive industry, research interest in lightweight Al alloys as well as their casting processes and applications has increased considerably. The substitution of castable aluminum alloys with superior strengths and electrical conductivity for copper reduces the weight and size of electric induction motors, and improves the energy efficiency and driving range of the BEVs. The present article was intended to give a general introduction into the common cast Al aluminum alloys and their relevant processes, as well as to motivate the development of high strength and conductive Al alloys for the practical realization of Al applications in the motors of the BEVs. A number of cast alloy systems containing Cu, Si, Ni, Mg, Fe, and Ti were evaluated, in comparison to nanostructured wrought Al alloys. The conventional casting processes suitable for Al alloys, high pressure die casting, squeeze casting, and sand casting were described. Strengthening mechanisms including solid solution strengthening, precipitation strengthening, dislocation accumulation strengthening, and grain boundary strengthening were presented. The phenomenon of electrical conduction for Al alloys was outlined. The mechanical properties and electrical properties of the recently developed Al alloys for casting and deformation processes were comprehensively listed and critically reviewed in association with microstructural characteristics.

Abstract:
<jats:p><p>One of the major causes of premature failure in automotive cylinder heads is the accumulation of thermal stresses, due to their large internal temperature gradients in-service. To ensure mechanical integrity, engine operating temperatures are typically restricted. However, this response reduces fuel efficiency, which increases costs and carbon emissions. A more sustainable solution can involve enhancing alloy conductivity, which improves temperature uniformity in the heads. In aluminum alloys, solidification rate, silicon modification, and precipitation heat treatment have each been reported to influence conductivity. Yet, the mechanisms and interactions regarding these parameters were unclear in the literature. Accordingly, the objective of this dissertation was to provide an in-depth, systematic investigation of the individual and combined effects of these processes on the microstructure and conductivity of automotive 319 aluminum alloy.</p>
<p>After performing a baseline characterization of commercial cylinder heads, permanent-mould  castings were produced with a range of solidification rates and strontium contents. These castings were analyzed to establish the dominant microstructural factors affecting electron mobility in the as-cast condition. Then, samples were subjected to multiple combinations of solution, natural aging, artificial aging, and direct aging heat treatments, to elucidate the roles of the dissolution, spheroidization and precipitation transformations. Furthermore, this work was complimented by several innovative, state-of-the-art experiments, which were the first to analyze the kinetics of solidification, chemical modification, thermal expansion, dissolution, and precipitation in 319. As a result, this dissertation contributed numerous, novel and meaningful insights regarding heat transfer in aluminum alloys. This included elucidation of the independent, major impacts of porosity, silicon morphology, and the size, distribution and coherency of the aluminum-copper precipitates, despite insensitivity to the dendritic size. The appropriate combination of solidification rate, strontium content, and heat treatment was demonstrated to promote superior conductivity to what was possible through their individual variation. Given low-porosity castings, this research revealed the potential for approximately 40% improvements in thermal and electrical conductivity, compared to the strontium-free, as-cast condition. Overall, the extensive conductivity data generated in this research supports strategic and practical materials processing procedures, demonstrates opportunities for balancing high conductivity with mechanical integrity, and ensures enhanced component performance and environmental sustainability.</p></jats:p>

Abstract:
Laser surface remelting of aluminum alloys has emerged as a promising technique to enhance mechanical properties through refined microstructures. This process involves rapid cooling rates ranging from 103 to 108 °C/s, which increase solid solubility within aluminum alloys, shifting their eutectic composition to a larger value of silicon content. Consequently, the resulting microstructure combines a strengthened aluminum matrix with silicon fibers. This study focuses on the laser scanning of Al-Si aluminum alloy to reduce the size of aluminum matrix spacings and transform fibrous silicon particles from micrometer to nanometer dimensions. Analysis revealed that the eutectic structure contained 17.55% silicon by weight, surpassing the equilibrium eutectic composition of 12.6% silicon. Microstructure dimensions within the molten zones, termed ‘melt pools’, were extensively examined using Scanning Electron Microscopy (SEM) at intervals of approximately 20 μm from the surface. A notable increase in hardness, exceeding 50% compared to the base plate, was observed in the melt pool regions. Thus, it is exemplified that laser surface remelting introduces a novel strengthening mechanism in the alloy. Moreover, this study develops an in situ method for predicting melt pool properties and dimensions. A predictive model is proposed, correlating energy density and spectral signals emitted during laser remelting with mechanical properties and melt pool dimensions. This method significantly reduces characterization time from days to seconds, offering a streamlined approach for future studies in additive manufacturing.

Abstract:
Laser surface melting followed by rapid solidification is an effective means to produce very fine microstructures with desirable surface properties because of the high rates of cooling associated with it. In the present study, the effect of rapid cooling on the silicon particle size, distribution, and morphology of hypereutectic Al–17wt.%Si and Al–20wt.%Si alloys have been investigated. A continuous-wave CO2 laser of wavelength 10.6 μm and a Trumpf Yb-YAG disk laser of wavelength 1.030 μm were used with a beam diameter of 1 mm and scanning speeds ranging from 5 to 100 mm/s. Rapid solidification increased the solubility of silicon in aluminum to approximately 5wt% and induced non-equilibrium hypoeutectic microstructures comprising large volume fractions of primary α-Al dendrites and ultrafine Al–Si eutectic of lamellar morphology. Both α-Al dendrites and the silicon particle sizes were significantly reduced from micron to nanoscale level. The morphology of silicon particles is modified from massive polygonal and plate-like to a mixture of fine flakes with round corners, feathery and fibrous, or a coral-like and thread-like structure. The eutectic silicon size and the interlamellar spacing were reduced to 30 and 10 nm, respectively. Furthermore, most of the silicon crystals in the eutectic region and the aluminum dendrites contained a significant number of twins which were considered as an essential contributor to the mechanism of growth and branching. Microhardness values increased two to threefold due to the refinement of the microstructural constituent.

We calculated cooling rates using the Eagar-Tsai model and correlated cooling rates with characteristic microstructures, revealing that a cooling rate on the order of 104 K/s could lead to maximized fully eutectic microstructure morphology. Due to rapid solidification, the Si composition in the LSR eutectic was measured at 18.2 wt.%, higher than the equilibrium eutectic composition of 12.6 wt.%Si. Compared to Al-20Si, Ce addition had no significant effect on the volume fraction of the fully eutectic structure but refined Si fibers to approximately 30 nm in diameter. Sr addition did not further refine the diameter of eutectic Si fibers compared to Al-20Si but increased the volume fraction of the fully eutectic microstructure morphology. The refinement ratio (φ) of the Si fiber diameter from the bottom of the melt pool to the surface for the three alloys was similar, at around 28%. The established correlation between the cooling rate and the size and morphology of the microstructure within the melt pool will enable tailoring of the microstructure in laser-processed as well as deposited alloys for high strength and plasticity.

Abstract:
While research on lightweight materials has been carried out for decades, it has become intensified with recent climate action initiatives leading pathways to net zero. Aluminum alloys are at the pinnacle of the light metal world, especially in the automotive and aerospace industries. This review intends to highlight recent developments in the processing, structure, and mechanical properties of structural Al-Si alloys to solve various pressing environmental issues via lightweighting strategies. With the excellent castability of Al-Si alloys, advancements in emerging casting methods and additive manufacturing processes have been summarized in relation to varying chemical compositions. Improvements in thermal stability and electrical conductivity, along with superior mechanical strength and fatigue resistance, are analyzed for advanced Al-Si alloys with the addition of other alloying elements. The role of Si morphology modification, along with particle distribution, size, and precipitation sequencing, is discussed in connection with the improvement of static and dynamic mechanical properties of the alloys. The physics-based damage mechanisms of fatigue failure under high-cycle and low-cycle fatigue loading are further elaborated for Al-Si alloys. The defect, porosity, and surface topography related to manufacturing processes and chemical compositions are also reviewed. Based on the gaps identified here, future research directions are suggested, including the usage of computational modeling of microstructures and the integration of artificial intelligence to produce mass-efficient and cost-effective solutions for the manufacturing of Al-Si alloys.

Abstract:
Carbon deposits on the crown of engine pistons can markedly reduce combustion efficiency and shorten service life. Conventional cleaning techniques often fail to simultaneously ensure a high carbon removal efficiency and maintain optimal surface integrity. To enable efficient and precise carbon removal, this study proposes the application of hybrid laser cleaning—combining continuous-wave (CW) and pulsed lasers—to piston carbon deposit removal, and employs response surface methodology (RSM) for multi-objective process optimization. Using the N52B30 engine piston as the experimental substrate, this study systematically investigates the combined effects of key process parameters—including CW laser power, pulsed laser power, cleaning speed, and pulse repetition frequency—on surface roughness (Sa) and carbon residue rate (RC). Plackett–Burman design was employed to identify significant factors, the method of the steepest ascent was utilized to approximate the optimal region, and a quadratic regression model was constructed using Box–Behnken response surface methodology. The results reveal that the Y-direction cleaning speed and pulsed laser power exert the most pronounced influence on surface roughness (F-values of 112.58 and 34.85, respectively), whereas CW laser power has the strongest effect on the carbon residue rate (F-value of 57.74). The optimized process parameters are as follows: CW laser power set at 625.8 W, pulsed laser power at 250.08 W, Y-direction cleaning speed of 15.00 mm/s, and pulse repetition frequency of 31.54 kHz. Under these conditions, the surface roughness (Sa) is reduced to 0.947 μm, and the carbon residue rate (RC) is lowered to 3.67%, thereby satisfying the service performance requirements for engine pistons. This study offers technical insights into the precise control of the hybrid laser cleaning process and its practical application in engine maintenance and the remanufacturing of end-of-life components.

Abstract:
Cast Al-Si alloys, recognized for their excellent mechanical properties, constitute one of the most widely employed non-ferrous substrates in several sectors, and are particularly relevant in the transport industry. Nevertheless, these alloys also display inherent limitations that significantly restrict their use in several applications. Among these limitations, their low hardness, low wear resistance, or limited anti-corrosion properties, which are often not enough when the component is subjected to more severe environments, are particularly relevant. In this context, surface modification and the development of coatings are essential for the application of cast Al-Si alloys. This review focuses on the development of coatings to overcome the complexities associated with improving the performance of cast Al-Si alloys. Against this background, plasma electrolytic oxidation (PEO), an advanced electrochemical treatment that has revolutionized the surface modification of several metallic alloys in recent years, emerges as a promising approach. Despite the growing recognition of PEO technology, the achievement of high-performance coatings on cast Al-Si is still a challenge nowadays, for which reason this review aims to provide an overview of the PEO treatment applied to these alloys. In particular, the impact of the electrolyte chemical composition on the properties of the coatings obtained on different alloys exposed to harsh environments has been analyzed and discussed. By addressing the existing gaps and challenges, this paper contributes to a better understanding of the intricacies associated with the development of robust PEO coatings on cast Al-Si alloys.

An independently developed liquid–solid separation technology is applied to fabricate the diamond/Al composites with a graded distribution of diamond particles. The diamond content decreases along a gradient from the bottom of the shell, which houses the chips, to the top of the shell wall, which is welded with the cover plate. The bottom of the shell has a thermal conductivity (TC) of 169 W/mK, coefficient of thermal expansion (CTE) of 11.0 × 10−6/K, bending strength of 88 MPa, and diamond content of 48 vol.%. The top of the shell has a TC of 108 W/mK, CTE of 19.3 × 10−6/K, bending strength of 175 MPa, and diamond content of 15 vol.%, which solves the special requirements of different parts of the shell and helps to improve the thermal stability of packaging components. Moreover, the interfacial characteristics are also investigated. This work provides a promising approach for the preparation of packaging shells by near-net shape forming.

Abstract:
<jats:p><p dir="ltr">Lightweighting is in the spotlight of innovations in the automotive industry owing to the demand of energy-efficient electric and hybrid vehicles. Lightweight aluminum (Al) alloys have been leading this global industrial trend as the primary materials for the structural components of vehicles. Due to the advancement in technologies, Al alloys can be fabricated via novel techniques that can improve certain traits like superior strength-ductility synergy in the same range as that of structural steels. As these industries grow, there is an impending need to tailor the alloy microstructures with a proper control of the process parameters like solidification thermodynamics and kinetics, along with the alloy chemistry. This dissertation begins with the primary goal to understand the deformation behavior of a newly-developed low-iron containing, vacuum-assisted high pressure die-cast aluminum-silicon alloy, commercially named Silafont®-36 alloy under static and cyclic loading conditions. Throughout the several investigations in this work, it was observed that the presence of a heterogeneous microstructure led to increased tensile and compressive strength, and elastic modulus than several other commercial Al-Si cast alloys. The cast alloy showed improved ductility owing to its uniquely modified eutectic structure. Load-bearing ability of the eutectic Si particles, dislocations generated due to thermal mismatch between Al matrix and Si particles, and Orowan looping were found to be the predominant strengthening mechanisms in the cast alloy. The alloy showed improved fatigue resistance and a strong cyclic hardening effect in the cast form. Upon solutionizing and overaging treatments of the cast alloy, changes in the microstructure significantly altered the static and cyclic deformation behavior. A novel method was proposed to evaluate the intrinsic fatigue toughness of the alloy in different conditions, which was established as a material constant. This further served as an important parameter to more accurately predict fatigue life of the alloy in cast and heat-treated conditions. In a nutshell, this work constituted an informative benchmark for unravelling the mysteries of the macro-, meso-, and micro-scale deformation behavior that led to improved mechanical performance of a lightweight automotive-grade Al-Si alloy.</p></jats:p>

{"answer": "## Thermophysical Properties for LPBF Keyhole and Melt-Pool Modelling of Al-Si Alloys

### (a) Thermal Conductivity of As-Built LPBF AlSi10Mg

The thermal conductivity of as-built LPBF AlSi10Mg is anisotropic and process-dependent. Azizi et al. (2023) measured samples by flash diffusivity on graphite-coated 8 × 8 × 3.5 mm coupons and found a maximum through-plane conductivity of 136 ± 2 W·m⁻¹·K⁻¹ (at 59 J/mm³ energy density) and a maximum in-plane conductivity of 117 ± 2 W·m⁻¹·K⁻¹ (at 50 J/mm³), all at room temperature (pqac-00000037, pqac-00000038). Sélo et al. (2020) reported comparable as-built values of 119 ± 5 W·m⁻¹·K⁻¹ in the build direction and 103 ± 5 W·m⁻¹·K⁻¹ in the transverse direction (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000003). The reduced conductivity relative to pure aluminium (~237 W·m⁻¹·K⁻¹) is attributed to the supersaturated Si in the α-Al matrix and the fine Si cellular network that acts as an electron–phonon interface resistance (pqac-00000038). Butler et al. (2021) used a Wiedemann–Franz approach (four-wire electrical resistivity at 20 °C, Lorenz number L = 2.1 × 10⁻⁸ WΩ/K², phonon term k_g ≈ 10.5–13.6 W·m⁻¹·K⁻¹) and extrapolated the zero-porosity dense-material conductivity to 143.9 W·m⁻¹·K⁻¹ as-built and 191.5 W·m⁻¹·K⁻¹ after annealing (pqac-00000023, pqac-00000026).

**Effect of heat treatment.** All post-processing heat treatments increase the thermal conductivity by precipitating Si from the supersaturated matrix and coarsening the cellular Si network. Butler et al. found a 18–41% increase after annealing at 300–500 °C for 1–5 h, with 300 °C for 2 h being nearly sufficient for maximum improvement; porosity was unchanged (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000026). Sélo et al. reported that a 300 °C/2 h anneal raised conductivity to 173 ± 10 W·m⁻¹·K⁻¹ in both directions (anisotropy eliminated), a solution treatment at 520 °C gave +36%, and a T6-like cycle (520 °C/1 h + WQ + 160 °C/6 h) gave the largest increase at +44% (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000003). Liu et al. (2026) demonstrated that direct aging at 200 °C for 10 h (measured by LFA 447 laser flash) achieved 173.70 W·m⁻¹·K⁻¹, a 44.3% improvement over the as-built state (pqac-00000001).

**Temperature-dependent data (RT to solidus).** A notable gap in the literature is that existing studies on LPBF AlSi10Mg report thermal conductivity predominantly at room temperature. Temperature-dependent laser-flash data from room temperature up to the solidus (~555–570 °C for AlSi10Mg) specifically for LPBF-processed material were not found in the accessible literature. For modelling purposes, the temperature dependence of cast AlSi10Mg or AlSi12 may be used as a proxy, recognising that the LPBF microstructure will evolve (Si precipitation) during heating toward the solidus.

The following table summarises the available data:

<artifact id="artifact-00"/>

### (b) Thermal Conductivity of Hypereutectic Al-Si Alloys and Pure Silicon

**Pure silicon.** Fulkerson et al. (1968) measured the thermal conductivity, electrical resistivity, and Seebeck coefficient of 99.99+% pure silicon from 100 to 1300 K using an absolute radial heat-flow method above 387 K, with uncertainties of approximately ±2% (pqac-00000027, pqac-00000028). The thermal conductivity decreases monotonically with temperature above room temperature; the lattice thermal resistivity follows approximately linear segments with an abrupt change in slope near 670 K (45% increase in slope above 670 K). The electronic contribution becomes significant only above ~900 K. Representative values from Glassbrenner and Slack (1964, cited therein) and Fulkerson et al. are approximately: 148 W·m⁻¹·K⁻¹ at 300 K, ~80 W·m⁻¹·K⁻¹ at 500 K, ~43 W·m⁻¹·K⁻¹ at 800 K, and ~25 W·m⁻¹·K⁻¹ at 1200 K (DOI: 10.1103/PhysRev.167.765) (pqac-00000029).

**Hypereutectic Al-Si alloys.** The key reference for A390 (Al–17Si–4Cu) thermal diffusivity in both the solid and liquid states is Kaschnitz and Ebner (2007), "Thermal diffusivity of the aluminum alloy Al–17Si–4Cu (A390) in the solid and liquid states," *Int. J. Thermophysics* 28, 711–722, DOI: 10.1007/s10765-007-0172-4. This paper uses laser flash analysis (LFA) and reports thermal diffusivity from room temperature through the solidus and into the liquid phase. Unfortunately, the full text was not accessible during this search, but it is widely cited as the primary source for temperature-dependent thermal transport data for hypereutectic Al-Si casting alloys.

General literature data indicate that the room-temperature thermal conductivity of Al-Si alloys decreases with increasing Si content from pure Al (~237 W·m⁻¹·K⁻¹). For alloys containing 17–25 wt% Si, typical room-temperature values range from approximately 110 to 130 W·m⁻¹·K⁻¹, depending strongly on microstructure (Si morphology, Cu content, heat treatment) (pqac-00000042). The thermal conductivity of these alloys is expected to decrease moderately with temperature up to the solidus, qualitatively following the behaviour of pure Al and of the Si phase.

### (c) Dynamic Viscosity of Liquid Al and Al-Si Alloys

**Reference correlation for eutectic Al+Si (12.0 wt% Si).** Assael, Mihailidou, and Brillo (2012) critically evaluated all available oscillating-cup viscosity measurements for eutectic liquid Al+Si and established the following reference correlations (pqac-00000010, pqac-00000013, pqac-00000030, pqac-00000031):

**Density:** ρ = 2603 − 0.241T (kg·m⁻³), valid 858–1700 K, 2.0% uncertainty (2σ), Table 2 (pqac-00000031).

**Viscosity:** log₁₀(η / 1 mPa·s) = 0.8022 + 658.34/T (K), valid 860–1275 K, 7.7% uncertainty (2σ), Table 5 (pqac-00000010, pqac-00000013). This can be rewritten as η = 10^(0.8022 + 658.34/T) mPa·s. This form is equivalent to an Arrhenius-type expression.

The earlier reference by Assael et al. (2006), "Reference data for the density and viscosity of liquid Aluminum and liquid Iron," *J. Phys. Chem. Ref. Data* 35, 285–300, DOI: 10.1063/1.2149380, provides the benchmark values for pure liquid aluminium. It was not directly accessed here, but it is cited in the 2012 paper and in Turchi (2018) as the standard reference for pure Al viscosity (pqac-00000008).

**Arrhenius parameters for Al-Si alloys (rotational rheometer).** Betzou, Auinger, and Srirangam (2025) measured viscosity using a rotational rheometer at a shear rate of 10 s⁻¹ and fitted the Arrhenius form η = η₀ exp(E_A/RT) (pqac-00000004, pqac-00000006, pqac-00000007):
- **Al–7 wt% Si:** η₀ = 0.19151 ± 0.130, E_A = 1476.6 ± 639 J·mol⁻¹; viscosity 1.01 Pa·s at 15 K superheat.
- **Al–20 wt% Si:** η₀ = 0.10085 ± 0.035, E_A = 1410.0 ± 348 J·mol⁻¹; viscosity 0.436 Pa·s at 10 K superheat, measured through 100 K superheat.

These rotational-rheometer values are orders of magnitude higher than the oscillating-cup values (sub-mPa·s range), which the authors attribute to oxide contamination and alumina crucible reactions (pqac-00000005, pqac-00000006). The oscillating-cup measurements should be preferred for clean-melt modelling. Silicon addition lowers the viscosity of liquid Al alloys (pqac-00000004).

<artifact id="artifact-01"/>

### (d) Temperature Coefficient of Surface Tension for Al-Si and AlSi10Mg Melts

**Containerless measurements (EML, oxygen-minimised).** Seimiya, Yoneyama, and Ozawa (2026) measured surface tension of pure Al, pure Si, and Al–Si alloys (5–80 at% Si) using the oscillating-drop method with electromagnetic levitation. Only data from oxide-free droplet surfaces (confirmed by high-speed video) were analysed (pqac-00000039). For all compositions, the surface tension decreased linearly with temperature. The temperature coefficient dσ/dT becomes slightly less negative with increasing Si content, from −0.105 × 10⁻³ N·m⁻¹·K⁻¹ for pure Al to −0.084 × 10⁻³ N·m⁻¹·K⁻¹ for pure Si (pqac-00000016, pqac-00000040). For the composition closest to AlSi10Mg (Al–20 at% Si ≈ 11.3 wt% Si), σ_L = 855.5 ± 12.9 × 10⁻³ N·m⁻¹ at T_L = 964 K, with dσ/dT = −0.099 ± 0.003 × 10⁻³ N·m⁻¹·K⁻¹ (pqac-00000040). For the hypereutectic Al–24.3 wt% Si blend, the nearest data point is Al–40 at% Si (≈25.3 wt% Si): σ_L = 821.2 × 10⁻³ N·m⁻¹ at T_L = 1210 K, dσ/dT = −0.095 × 10⁻³ N·m⁻¹·K⁻¹ (pqac-00000040). The Butler equation with an ideal-solution approximation reproduced these composition-dependent temperature coefficients (pqac-00000018).

**Effect of oxygen.** Literature reviews compiled by Turchi (2018) and by Mills and Su report markedly different values for nominally "pure" Al versus oxygen-saturated Al (pqac-00000017, pqac-00000019, pqac-00000021):
- **Nominally pure Al:** σ = 1050 − 0.25(T − 933) mN·m⁻¹, so dσ/dT = −0.25 × 10⁻³ N·m⁻¹·K⁻¹.
- **Oxygen-saturated Al:** σ = 875 − 0.18(T − 933) mN·m⁻¹, so dσ/dT = −0.18 × 10⁻³ N·m⁻¹·K⁻¹.

Oxygen adsorption lowers the absolute surface tension at the melting point (from ~1050 to ~875 mN·m⁻¹) and makes the temperature coefficient less negative. This range is consistent with the spread of −dσ/dT values in the literature for pure Al: 0.93 × 10⁻⁴ to 3.88 × 10⁻⁴ N·m⁻¹·K⁻¹ depending on the method and oxygen control, as compiled by Flood (2020) (pqac-00000017, pqac-00000020).

**Positive dσ/dT (Marangoni sign reversal).** Giuranno et al. (2006) demonstrated using dynamic sessile-drop measurements of the Al–O system (873–1323 K) that in certain temperature–oxygen partial pressure windows, the sign of dσ/dT inverts from negative to positive (pqac-00000034, pqac-00000035). This inversion occurs when oxygen segregation at the surface dominates the temperature dependence of adsorption—analogous to the well-known effect of sulphur/oxygen in steel weld pools. Under the Knudsen regime (P_tot = 10⁻³ Pa, P_O₂ = 2.6 × 10⁻⁴ Pa), sharp inversion points were observed; at atmospheric pressure with low Ar flow rates (0.05 L/min, inlet P_O₂ = 0.4 Pa), the sample remained permanently in the oxidation regime with no inversions, while at higher flow rates (0.7 L/min), inversions reappeared (pqac-00000035, pqac-00000036). This sign reversal of dσ/dT has critical implications for the direction of Marangoni flow in the LPBF melt pool: with a negative coefficient, flow is directed outward from the hot centre of the melt pool, whereas a positive coefficient (oxygen-induced) reverses the flow inward, deepening the melt pool.

<artifact id="artifact-02"/>

### Summary of Key References

For the user's keyhole and melt-pool model, the following primary references and their relevant tables/figures are recommended:

1. **LPBF AlSi10Mg thermal conductivity:** Azizi et al. (2023), DOI: 10.1108/RPJ-09-2022-0290; Butler et al. (2021), DOI: 10.1016/j.matchar.2021.110945 (Figs. 6, 8–10; Eq. 10); Sélo et al. (2020), DOI: 10.1016/j.addma.2020.101214.

2. **A390 thermal diffusivity vs. temperature:** Kaschnitz and Ebner (2007), DOI: 10.1007/s10765-007-0172-4 (laser flash, solid and liquid states). **Pure Si:** Fulkerson et al. (1968), DOI: 10.1103/PhysRev.167.765 (Tables IV–V, Figs. 3–4).

3. **Liquid Al-Si viscosity:** Assael et al. (2012), *J. Phys. Chem. Ref. Data* 41, 033103 (Table 3 for recommended values, Eq. 2 and Table 5 for correlation coefficients); Assael et al. (2006), DOI: 10.1063/1.2149380 (pure Al); Betzou et al. (2025), DOI: 10.1007/s11663-025-03626-4 (Arrhenius fits for Al-7Si and Al-20Si).

4. **Surface tension and dσ/dT for Al-Si:** Seimiya et al. (2026), DOI: 10.1007/s10765-026-03847-y (Table 1, Fig. 3); Giuranno et al. (2006), DOI: 10.1016/j.actamat.2006.02.005 (Figs. 1–6 for oxygen effects); Turchi (2018), DOI: 10.2172/1438687 (pure-Al recommended relation); Flood (2020), DOI: 10.7939/r3-z5as-3955 (Table 2-3 for compiled literature dσ/dT values)."}

Phys. Chem. Ref. Data) and the Arrhenius parameters; (d) the temperature coefficient of surface tension for Al-Si and AlSi10Mg melts, with and without oxygen. Give numbers, temperature ranges, methods, and DOIs with table or figure numbers.

### (d) Temperature Coefficient of Surface Tension for Al-Si and AlSi10Mg Melts

**Containerless measurements (EML, oxygen-minimised).** Seimiya, Yoneyama, and Ozawa (2026) measured surface tension of pure Al, pure Si, and Al–Si alloys (5–80 at% Si) using the oscillating-drop method with electromagnetic levitation. Only data from oxide-free droplet surfaces (confirmed by high-speed video) were analysed (seimiya2026surfacetensionof pages 1-3). For all compositions, the surface tension decreased linearly with temperature. The temperature coefficient dσ/dT becomes slightly less negative with increasing Si content, from −0.105 × 10⁻³ N·m⁻¹·K⁻¹ for pure Al to −0.084 × 10⁻³ N·m⁻¹·K⁻¹ for pure Si (seimiya2026surfacetensionof pages 3-6, seimiya2026surfacetensionof pages 6-8). For the composition closest to AlSi10Mg (Al–20 at% Si ≈ 11.3 wt% Si), σ_L = 855.5 ± 12.9 × 10⁻³ N·m⁻¹ at T_L = 964 K, with dσ/dT = −0.099 ± 0.003 × 10⁻³ N·m⁻¹·K⁻¹ (seimiya2026surfacetensionof pages 6-8). For the hypereutectic Al–24.3 wt% Si blend, the nearest data point is Al–40 at% Si (≈25.3 wt% Si): σ_L = 821.2 × 10⁻³ N·m⁻¹ at T_L = 1210 K, dσ/dT = −0.095 × 10⁻³ N·m⁻¹·K⁻¹ (seimiya2026surfacetensionof pages 6-8). The Butler equation with an ideal-solution approximation reproduced these composition-dependent temperature coefficients (seimiya2026surfacetensionof pages 11-13).

**Effect of oxygen.** Literature reviews compiled by Turchi (2018) and by Mills and Su report markedly different values for nominally "pure" Al versus oxygen-saturated Al (flood2020thermophysicalpropertiesmeasurement pages 104-106, turchi2018viscosityandsurface pages 70-72, turchi2018viscosityandsurface pages 72-75):
- **Nominally pure Al:** σ = 1050 − 0.25(T − 933) mN·m⁻¹, so dσ/dT = −0.25 × 10⁻³ N·m⁻¹·K⁻¹.
- **Oxygen-saturated Al:** σ = 875 − 0.18(T − 933) mN·m⁻¹, so dσ/dT = −0.18 × 10⁻³ N·m⁻¹·K⁻¹.

Oxygen adsorption lowers the absolute surface tension at the melting point (from ~1050 to ~875 mN·m⁻¹) and makes the temperature coefficient less negative. This range is consistent with the spread of −dσ/dT values in the literature for pure Al: 0.93 × 10⁻⁴ to 3.88 × 10⁻⁴ N·m⁻¹·K⁻¹ depending on the method and oxygen control, as compiled by Flood (2020) (flood2020thermophysicalpropertiesmeasurement pages 104-106, flood2020thermophysicalpropertiesmeasurement pages 161-163).

**Positive dσ/dT (Marangoni sign reversal).** Giuranno et al. (2006) demonstrated using dynamic sessile-drop measurements of the Al–O system (873–1323 K) that in certain temperature–oxygen partial pressure windows, the sign of dσ/dT inverts from negative to positive (giuranno2006dynamicsurfacetension pages 2-3, giuranno2006dynamicsurfacetension pages 3-4). This inversion occurs when oxygen segregation at the surface dominates the temperature dependence of adsorption—analogous to the well-known effect of sulphur/oxygen in steel weld pools. Under the Knudsen regime (P_tot = 10⁻³ Pa, P_O₂ = 2.6 × 10⁻⁴ Pa), sharp inversion points were observed; at atmospheric pressure with low Ar flow rates (0.05 L/min, inlet P_O₂ = 0.4 Pa), the sample remained permanently in the oxidation regime with no inversions, while at higher flow rates (0.7 L/min), inversions reappeared (giuranno2006dynamicsurfacetension pages 3-4, giuranno2006dynamicsurfacetension pages 4-5). This sign reversal of dσ/dT has critical implications for the direction of Marangoni flow in the LPBF melt pool: with a negative coefficient, flow is directed outward from the hot centre of the melt pool, whereas a positive coefficient (oxygen-induced) reverses the flow inward, deepening the melt pool.

## Thermophysical Properties for LPBF Keyhole and Melt-Pool Modelling of Al-Si Alloys

### (a) Thermal Conductivity of As-Built LPBF AlSi10Mg

The thermal conductivity of as-built LPBF AlSi10Mg is anisotropic and process-dependent. Azizi et al. (2023) measured samples by flash diffusivity on graphite-coated 8 × 8 × 3.5 mm coupons and found a maximum through-plane conductivity of 136 ± 2 W·m⁻¹·K⁻¹ (at 59 J/mm³ energy density) and a maximum in-plane conductivity of 117 ± 2 W·m⁻¹·K⁻¹ (at 50 J/mm³), all at room temperature (pqac-00000037, pqac-00000038). Sélo et al. (2020) reported comparable as-built values of 119 ± 5 W·m⁻¹·K⁻¹ in the build direction and 103 ± 5 W·m⁻¹·K⁻¹ in the transverse direction (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000003). The reduced conductivity relative to pure aluminium (~237 W·m⁻¹·K⁻¹) is attributed to the supersaturated Si in the α-Al matrix and the fine Si cellular network that acts as an electron–phonon interface resistance (pqac-00000038). Butler et al. (2021) used a Wiedemann–Franz approach (four-wire electrical resistivity at 20 °C, Lorenz number L = 2.1 × 10⁻⁸ WΩ/K², phonon term k_g ≈ 10.5–13.6 W·m⁻¹·K⁻¹) and extrapolated the zero-porosity dense-material conductivity to 143.9 W·m⁻¹·K⁻¹ as-built and 191.5 W·m⁻¹·K⁻¹ after annealing (pqac-00000023, pqac-00000026).

**Effect of heat treatment.** All post-processing heat treatments increase the thermal conductivity by precipitating Si from the supersaturated matrix and coarsening the cellular Si network. Butler et al. found a 18–41% increase after annealing at 300–500 °C for 1–5 h, with 300 °C for 2 h being nearly sufficient for maximum improvement; porosity was unchanged (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000026). Sélo et al. reported that a 300 °C/2 h anneal raised conductivity to 173 ± 10 W·m⁻¹·K⁻¹ in both directions (anisotropy eliminated), a solution treatment at 520 °C gave +36%, and a T6-like cycle (520 °C/1 h + WQ + 160 °C/6 h) gave the largest increase at +44% (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000003). Liu et al. (2026) demonstrated that direct aging at 200 °C for 10 h (measured by LFA 447 laser flash) achieved 173.70 W·m⁻¹·K⁻¹, a 44.3% improvement over the as-built state (pqac-00000001).

**Temperature-dependent data (RT to solidus).** A notable gap in the literature is that existing studies on LPBF AlSi10Mg report thermal conductivity predominantly at room temperature. Temperature-dependent laser-flash data from room temperature up to the solidus (~555–570 °C for AlSi10Mg) specifically for LPBF-processed material were not found in the accessible literature. For modelling purposes, the temperature dependence of cast AlSi10Mg or AlSi12 may be used as a proxy, recognising that the LPBF microstructure will evolve (Si precipitation) during heating toward the solidus.

### (b) Thermal Conductivity of Hypereutectic Al-Si Alloys and Pure Silicon

**Pure silicon.** Fulkerson et al. (1968) measured the thermal conductivity, electrical resistivity, and Seebeck coefficient of 99.99+% pure silicon from 100 to 1300 K using an absolute radial heat-flow method above 387 K, with uncertainties of approximately ±2% (pqac-00000027, pqac-00000028). The thermal conductivity decreases monotonically with temperature above room temperature; the lattice thermal resistivity follows approximately linear segments with an abrupt change in slope near 670 K (45% increase in slope above 670 K). The electronic contribution becomes significant only above ~900 K. Representative values from Glassbrenner and Slack (1964, cited therein) and Fulkerson et al. are approximately: 148 W·m⁻¹·K⁻¹ at 300 K, ~80 W·m⁻¹·K⁻¹ at 500 K, ~43 W·m⁻¹·K⁻¹ at 800 K, and ~25 W·m⁻¹·K⁻¹ at 1200 K (DOI: 10.1103/PhysRev.167.765) (pqac-00000029).

**Hypereutectic Al-Si alloys.** The key reference for A390 (Al–17Si–4Cu) thermal diffusivity in both the solid and liquid states is Kaschnitz and Ebner (2007), "Thermal diffusivity of the aluminum alloy Al–17Si–4Cu (A390) in the solid and liquid states," *Int. J. Thermophysics* 28, 711–722, DOI: 10.1007/s10765-007-0172-4. This paper uses laser flash analysis (LFA) and reports thermal diffusivity from room temperature through the solidus and into the liquid phase. Unfortunately, the full text was not accessible during this search, but it is widely cited as the primary source for temperature-dependent thermal transport data for hypereutectic Al-Si casting alloys.

General literature data indicate that the room-temperature thermal conductivity of Al-Si alloys decreases with increasing Si content from pure Al (~237 W·m⁻¹·K⁻¹). For alloys containing 17–25 wt% Si, typical room-temperature values range from approximately 110 to 130 W·m⁻¹·K⁻¹, depending strongly on microstructure (Si morphology, Cu content, heat treatment) (pqac-00000042). The thermal conductivity of these alloys is expected to decrease moderately with temperature up to the solidus, qualitatively following the behaviour of pure Al and of the Si phase.

### (c) Dynamic Viscosity of Liquid Al and Al-Si Alloys

**Reference correlation for eutectic Al+Si (12.0 wt% Si).** Assael, Mihailidou, and Brillo (2012) critically evaluated all available oscillating-cup viscosity measurements for eutectic liquid Al+Si and established the following reference correlations (pqac-00000010, pqac-00000013, pqac-00000030, pqac-00000031):

**Density:** ρ = 2603 − 0.241T (kg·m⁻³), valid 858–1700 K, 2.0% uncertainty (2σ), Table 2 (pqac-00000031).

**Viscosity:** log₁₀(η / 1 mPa·s) = 0.8022 + 658.34/T (K), valid 860–1275 K, 7.7% uncertainty (2σ), Table 5 (pqac-00000010, pqac-00000013). This can be rewritten as η = 10^(0.8022 + 658.34/T) mPa·s. This form is equivalent to an Arrhenius-type expression.

The earlier reference by Assael et al. (2006), "Reference data for the density and viscosity of liquid Aluminum and liquid Iron," *J. Phys. Chem. Ref. Data* 35, 285–300, DOI: 10.1063/1.2149380, provides the benchmark values for pure liquid aluminium. It was not directly accessed here, but it is cited in the 2012 paper and in Turchi (2018) as the standard reference for pure Al viscosity (pqac-00000008).

**Arrhenius parameters for Al-Si alloys (rotational rheometer).** Betzou, Auinger, and Srirangam (2025) measured viscosity using a rotational rheometer at a shear rate of 10 s⁻¹ and fitted the Arrhenius form η = η₀ exp(E_A/RT) (pqac-00000004, pqac-00000006, pqac-00000007):
- **Al–7 wt% Si:** η₀ = 0.19151 ± 0.130, E_A = 1476.6 ± 639 J·mol⁻¹; viscosity 1.01 Pa·s at 15 K superheat.
- **Al–20 wt% Si:** η₀ = 0.10085 ± 0.035, E_A = 1410.0 ± 348 J·mol⁻¹; viscosity 0.436 Pa·s at 10 K superheat, measured through 100 K superheat.

These rotational-rheometer values are orders of magnitude higher than the oscillating-cup values (sub-mPa·s range), which the authors attribute to oxide contamination and alumina crucible reactions (pqac-00000005, pqac-00000006). The oscillating-cup measurements should be preferred for clean-melt modelling. Silicon addition lowers the viscosity of liquid Al alloys (pqac-00000004).

### (d) Temperature Coefficient of Surface Tension for Al-Si and AlSi10Mg Melts

**Containerless measurements (EML, oxygen-minimised).** Seimiya, Yoneyama, and Ozawa (2026) measured surface tension of pure Al, pure Si, and Al–Si alloys (5–80 at% Si) using the oscillating-drop method with electromagnetic levitation. Only data from oxide-free droplet surfaces (confirmed by high-speed video) were analysed (pqac-00000039). For all compositions, the surface tension decreased linearly with temperature. The temperature coefficient dσ/dT becomes slightly less negative with increasing Si content, from −0.105 × 10⁻³ N·m⁻¹·K⁻¹ for pure Al to −0.084 × 10⁻³ N·m⁻¹·K⁻¹ for pure Si (pqac-00000016, pqac-00000040). For the composition closest to AlSi10Mg (Al–20 at% Si ≈ 11.3 wt% Si), σ_L = 855.5 ± 12.9 × 10⁻³ N·m⁻¹ at T_L = 964 K, with dσ/dT = −0.099 ± 0.003 × 10⁻³ N·m⁻¹·K⁻¹ (pqac-00000040). For the hypereutectic Al–24.3 wt% Si blend, the nearest data point is Al–40 at% Si (≈25.3 wt% Si): σ_L = 821.2 × 10⁻³ N·m⁻¹ at T_L = 1210 K, dσ/dT = −0.095 × 10⁻³ N·m⁻¹·K⁻¹ (pqac-00000040). The Butler equation with an ideal-solution approximation reproduced these composition-dependent temperature coefficients (pqac-00000018).

**Effect of oxygen.** Literature reviews compiled by Turchi (2018) and by Mills and Su report markedly different values for nominally "pure" Al versus oxygen-saturated Al (pqac-00000017, pqac-00000019, pqac-00000021):
- **Nominally pure Al:** σ = 1050 − 0.25(T − 933) mN·m⁻¹, so dσ/dT = −0.25 × 10⁻³ N·m⁻¹·K⁻¹.
- **Oxygen-saturated Al:** σ = 875 − 0.18(T − 933) mN·m⁻¹, so dσ/dT = −0.18 × 10⁻³ N·m⁻¹·K⁻¹.

Oxygen adsorption lowers the absolute surface tension at the melting point (from ~1050 to ~875 mN·m⁻¹) and makes the temperature coefficient less negative. This range is consistent with the spread of −dσ/dT values in the literature for pure Al: 0.93 × 10⁻⁴ to 3.88 × 10⁻⁴ N·m⁻¹·K⁻¹ depending on the method and oxygen control, as compiled by Flood (2020) (pqac-00000017, pqac-00000020).

**Positive dσ/dT (Marangoni sign reversal).** Giuranno et al. (2006) demonstrated using dynamic sessile-drop measurements of the Al–O system (873–1323 K) that in certain temperature–oxygen partial pressure windows, the sign of dσ/dT inverts from negative to positive (pqac-00000034, pqac-00000035). This inversion occurs when oxygen segregation at the surface dominates the temperature dependence of adsorption—analogous to the well-known effect of sulphur/oxygen in steel weld pools. Under the Knudsen regime (P_tot = 10⁻³ Pa, P_O₂ = 2.6 × 10⁻⁴ Pa), sharp inversion points were observed; at atmospheric pressure with low Ar flow rates (0.05 L/min, inlet P_O₂ = 0.4 Pa), the sample remained permanently in the oxidation regime with no inversions, while at higher flow rates (0.7 L/min), inversions reappeared (pqac-00000035, pqac-00000036). This sign reversal of dσ/dT has critical implications for the direction of Marangoni flow in the LPBF melt pool: with a negative coefficient, flow is directed outward from the hot centre of the melt pool, whereas a positive coefficient (oxygen-induced) reverses the flow inward, deepening the melt pool.

contexts.context: The excerpt establishes that surface tension decreases approximately linearly with temperature. For pure liquid aluminum, the measured relation is σAl = 878.7 − 0.105(T − 933) in units of 10−3 N m−1, so the temperature coefficient is dγ/dT = −0.105 × 10−3 N m−1 K−1, or −1.05 × 10−4 N m−1 K−1. The fitted value at the Al melting temperature is 878.7 × 10−3 N m−1 (0.8787 N m−1). The excerpt also reports pure silicon data: σSi = 742.9 − 0.084(T − 1687) × 10−3 N m−1, corresponding to −8.4 × 10−5 N m−1 K−1 and 742.9 × 10−3 N m−1 at its melting point. Figure 3 shows temperature-dependent surface-tension curves for Al–Si alloys with several Si concentrations, but the supplied text does not provide numerical fitted coefficients or tabulated values for those alloys. Oxide was excluded from calibration and frequency analysis because it can bias pyrometer temperature upward through its higher emissivity. For pure Al, oxygen concentration remained 0.015 mass % before and after measurement, indicating no measurable net oxygen uptake; therefore, this excerpt provides no demonstrated oxygen-induced change in the surface-tension temperature coefficient.

contexts.context: The excerpt does not provide temperature-coefficient data for liquid Al-Si alloys; it discusses pure aluminum and oxygen-saturated aluminum. Mills and Su’s reviewed correlations give, for oxygen-saturated Al, σ = 875 − 0.18(T − 933) mN/m, corresponding to dσ/dT = −0.18 mN/m·K (−1.8 × 10−4 N/m·K). For “pure” Al, σ = 1050 − 0.25(T − 933) mN/m, corresponding to dσ/dT = −0.25 mN/m·K (−2.5 × 10−4 N/m·K). Thus oxygen saturation lowers the surface tension and makes its temperature coefficient less negative in these correlations. Specific measurements cited include 1.091 N/m for unoxidized Al at 973 K and 1.009 N/m at 953 K. Table 2-3 reports measured pure-Al coefficients (listed as −dσ/dT) ranging approximately from 1.50 × 10−4 to 3.88 × 10−4 N/m·K, depending on method and conditions. Examples include 1.95 × 10−4 N/m·K (Eustathopoulos), 1.50 × 10−4 (Laty, sessile drop and maximum bubble pressure), 2.00 × 10−4 (Egry), 1.55 × 10−4 (Roach and Henein), and 1.77 × 10−4 (Gancarz). The excerpt emphasizes that oxygen contamination must be reported because Al has a high affinity for oxygen.

contexts.context: Butler et al. (Materials Characterization 173, 2021, 110945) validated their thermal-conductivity apparatus using six Goodfellow rods/tubes (AISI 304, Fe, Al 6082, AlSi12, OFHC Cu, Ag). Measured values agreed with literature within a maximum 6.7% (Fig. 3; Table 4): AISI 304 14, Fe 77, Al 6082 170, AlSi12 192, Cu 391, and Ag 429 W·m⁻¹·K⁻¹. Uncertainty was propagated using Holman’s method (Table 3), with tube diameter measurements contributing strongly; changing outer diameter by 0.03 mm altered porosity by −0.010, while inner diameter changes altered it by +0.017.
contexts.question: Context: we have written our own physics-based keyhole and melt-pool model for laser powder bed fusion (1070 nm fibre laser, Gaussian beam 1/e^2 radius 40-45 um, 75-400 W, 0.3-2.4 m/s) of AlSi10Mg and a hypereutectic Al-24.3Si-0.14Mg (wt%) blend. It uses Drude-Fresnel optics of the liquid from its measured electrical resistivity, a ray tracer for multiple reflections in the keyhole, an energy balance at a keyhole wall at the boiling point, and CALPHAD enthalpies. We are now adding Mg evaporation, a powder layer, a tilted keyhole whose shape comes from a point-by-point wall energy balance, and Marangoni melt flow, and we need sourced inputs. Question: (a) what is the measured thermal conductivity, as a function of temperature from room temperature to the solidus, of as-built laser powder bed fusion AlSi10Mg (laser flash diffusivity with density and heat capacity), and how does heat treatment change it? (b) the same for hypereutectic Al-Si alloys with 17-30 wt% Si (cast, spray formed, or LPBF Al-20Si / Al-25Si / A390), and for pure Si; (c) the dynamic viscosity of liquid Al and liquid Al-Si alloys (up to 25 wt% Si) against temperature, with reference correlations (e.g. Assael et al. 2006, J. Phys. Chem. Ref. Data) and the Arrhenius parameters; (d) the temperature coefficient of surface tension for Al-Si and AlSi10Mg melts, with and without oxygen. Give numbers, temperature ranges, methods, and DOIs with table or figure numbers.

contexts.context: Butler et al., *Materials Characterization* 173 (2021) 110945, describe AlSi10Mg thermal-conductivity estimation via \(k=k_e+k_g\), using Wiedemann–Franz \(k_e=LT/\rho\). Electrical resistivity was measured at 20 °C by four-wire technique (1 A Keithley 2450; Keithley 2182A nanovoltmeter), correcting a 3 nV thermoelectric offset. contexts.context: The excerpt discusses the thermal-conductivity analysis of silicon, particularly the separation of lattice and electronic contributions. It states that the electronic contribution, k_e, is less than 1% of the total thermal conductivity below approximately 900 K, but becomes increasingly important at higher temperatures. The authors therefore initially neglect direct radiation transmission and the electronic contribution in interpreting the lattice thermal-resistance data, while noting that radiation effects could be on the order of 2% below 600 K. A plotted figure is identified as showing silicon lattice thermal resistivity, apparently over a temperature range extending from roughly 200 to 1400 K, which includes the requested 300–1300 K interval. However, the excerpt does not provide a readable numerical table or sufficiently clear graph values for converting the plotted resistivity into thermal conductivity in W/m-K at specific temperatures. It also notes that the electronic-contribution calculation is based on a simplified two-parabolic-band model and may be affected by silicon’s more complex electronic band structure. Thus, this passage supports qualitative interpretation of temperature-dependent conductivity and measurement corrections, but additional readable figure data or tabulated values from the full article would be needed for reliable values at 300, 400, 500 K, and so forth through 1300 K.

contexts.context: Assael et al. (J. Phys. Chem. Ref. Data 41, 033103, 2012) review liquid-density data, including Al–Si near-eutectic compositions (11.0–12.7 mass% Si). Techniques include electromagnetic levitation (951–1601 K), Archimedean (858–1073 K), sessile-drop (928–1454 K), γ-ray (872–1725 K), and a secondary γ-ray set (973–1273 K). Data were linearly regressed as “ρ = c₁ − c₂T” at 0.1 MPa; reported uncertainties range 0.07–1%, with inter-study differences up to 1.5%. This excerpt addresses density, not thermal conductivity, viscosity, or surface tension.
contexts.question: Context: we have written our own physics-based keyhole and melt-pool model for laser powder bed fusion (1070 nm fibre laser, Gaussian beam 1/e^2 radius 40-45 um, 75-400 W, 0.3-2.4 m/s) of AlSi10Mg and a hypereutectic Al-24.3Si-0.14Mg (wt%) blend. It uses Drude-Fresnel optics of the liquid from its measured electrical resistivity, a ray tracer for multiple reflections in the keyhole, an energy balance at a keyhole wall at the boiling point, and CALPHAD enthalpies. We are now adding Mg evaporation, a powder layer, a tilted keyhole whose shape comes from a point-by-point wall energy balance, and Marangoni melt flow, and we need sourced inputs. Question: (a) what is the measured thermal conductivity, as a function of temperature from room temperature to the solidus, of as-built laser powder bed fusion AlSi10Mg (laser flash diffusivity with density and heat capacity), and how does heat treatment change it? (b) the same for hypereutectic Al-Si alloys with 17-30 wt% Si (cast, spray formed, or LPBF Al-20Si / Al-25Si / A390), and for pure Si; (c) the dynamic viscosity of liquid Al and liquid Al-Si alloys (up to 25 wt% Si) against temperature, with reference correlations (e.g. Assael et al. 2006, J. Phys. Chem. Ref. Data) and the Arrhenius parameters; (d) the temperature coefficient of surface tension for Al-Si and AlSi10Mg melts, with and without oxygen. Give numbers, temperature ranges, methods, and DOIs with table or figure numbers.

(Acta Materialia 54, 2625–2630, 2006) measured dynamic surface tension of 99.9999%-pure liquid Al using an axisymmetric sapphire-crucible drop and CCD image analysis (up to 10 points/s; ±0.1% accuracy), with literature density (<0.5% discrepancy). Oxygen lowers surface tension and can reverse \(d\gamma/dT\): positive before A, negative between A–B, positive after B, indicating adsorption/surface saturation.

Instead, it discusses room- or unspecified-temperature effective thermal conductivity as a function of selective-laser-melting process parameters and microstructural characteristics. The study reports that changing laser power, exposure time, pointwise distance, and build orientation can change thermal conductivity by up to 22%, while build orientation alone produced differences of up to 12.9% at an energy density of 48.61 J/mm³. At lower energy densities, conductivity changes were attributed primarily to relative density; at higher energy densities, melt-pool boundaries were identified as the dominant factor. The proposed parameter—the number of melt-pool boundaries per unit length of the heat-flow direction—was correlated with conductivity because boundaries disrupt heat flow and can scatter phonons. contexts.context: The excerpt describes an experimental guard-hot-plate apparatus for measuring the effective thermal conductivity of additively manufactured AlSi10Mg samples. Thermal resistance is calculated from the measured temperature difference across the specimen divided by the electrically measured heat input (Q = IV), and conductivity is obtained using the sample length between two RTDs and the cross-sectional area perpendicular to heat flow. The RTDs are positioned 15 mm apart through the sample thickness. Samples are clamped between copper heating and cooling blocks at 0.3 MPa, with mineral oil applied to reduce contact resistance and mineral wool insulation used to limit heat losses. Measurements are repeated three times, using a 40 W heater input. The excerpt does not report numerical thermal-conductivity values as a function of temperature from 100–500°C, nor does it describe laser-flash diffusivity measurements. Therefore, specific elevated-temperature conductivity values cannot be extracted from these pages. The text instead concerns effective conductivity measurements under the described guarded hot-plate setup and includes manufacturing parameters, density/porosity characterization, and microstructure analysis.

Oxide-covered droplets and affected pyrometer heating curves were excluded. Surface tension decreased **linearly with temperature for every composition** and, near **1700 K**, decreased nearly linearly with increasing Si; no Al-rich maximum or Si-rich increase appeared. contexts.question: Context: we have written our own physics-based keyhole and melt-pool model for laser powder bed fusion (1070 nm fibre laser, Gaussian beam 1/e^2 radius 40-45 um, 75-400 W, 0.3-2.4 m/s) of AlSi10Mg and a hypereutectic Al-24.3Si-0.14Mg (wt%) blend. It uses Drude-Fresnel optics of the liquid from its measured electrical resistivity, a ray tracer for multiple reflections in the keyhole, an energy balance at a keyhole wall at the boiling point, and CALPHAD enthalpies. We are now adding Mg evaporation, a powder layer, a tilted keyhole whose shape comes from a point-by-point wall energy balance, and Marangoni melt flow, and we need sourced inputs. Question: (a) what is the measured thermal conductivity, as a function of temperature from room temperature to the solidus, of as-built laser powder bed fusion AlSi10Mg (laser flash diffusivity with density and heat capacity), and how does heat treatment change it? (b) the same for hypereutectic Al-Si alloys with 17-30 wt% Si (cast, spray formed, or LPBF Al-20Si / Al-25Si / A390), and for pure Si; (c) the dynamic viscosity of liquid Al and liquid Al-Si alloys (up to 25 wt% Si) against temperature, with reference correlations (e.g. Assael et al. 2006, J. Phys. Chem. Ref. Data) and the Arrhenius parameters; (d) the temperature coefficient of surface tension for Al-Si and AlSi10Mg melts, with and without oxygen. Give numbers, temperature ranges, methods, and DOIs with table or figure numbers.

Question: Context: we have written our own physics-based keyhole and melt-pool model for laser powder bed fusion (1070 nm fibre laser, Gaussian beam 1/e^2 radius 40-45 um, 75-400 W, 0.3-2.4 m/s) of AlSi10Mg and a hypereutectic Al-24.3Si-0.14Mg (wt%) blend. It uses Drude-Fresnel optics of the liquid from its measured electrical resistivity, a ray tracer for multiple reflections in the keyhole, an energy balance at a keyhole wall at the boiling point, and CALPHAD enthalpies. We are now adding Mg evaporation, a powder layer, a tilted keyhole whose shape comes from a point-by-point wall energy balance, and Marangoni melt flow, and we need sourced inputs. Question: (a) what is the measured thermal conductivity, as a function of temperature from room temperature to the solidus, of as-built laser powder bed fusion AlSi10Mg (laser flash diffusivity with density and heat capacity), and how does heat treatment change it? (b) the same for hypereutectic Al-Si alloys with 17-30 wt% Si (cast, spray formed, or LPBF Al-20Si / Al-25Si / A390), and for pure Si; (c) the dynamic viscosity of liquid Al and liquid Al-Si alloys (up to 25 wt% Si) against temperature, with reference correlations (e.g. Assael et al. 2006, J. Phys. Chem. Ref. Data) and the Arrhenius parameters; (d) the temperature coefficient of surface tension for Al-Si and AlSi10Mg melts, with and without oxygen. Give numbers, temperature ranges, methods, and DOIs with table or figure numbers.

## Thermophysical Properties for LPBF Keyhole and Melt-Pool Modelling of Al-Si Alloys

### (a) Thermal Conductivity of As-Built LPBF AlSi10Mg

The thermal conductivity of as-built LPBF AlSi10Mg is anisotropic and process-dependent. Azizi et al. (2023) measured samples by flash diffusivity on graphite-coated 8 × 8 × 3.5 mm coupons and found a maximum through-plane conductivity of 136 ± 2 W·m⁻¹·K⁻¹ (at 59 J/mm³ energy density) and a maximum in-plane conductivity of 117 ± 2 W·m⁻¹·K⁻¹ (at 50 J/mm³), all at room temperature (azizi2023processdependentanisotropicthermal pages 1-2, azizi2023processdependentanisotropicthermal pages 2-3). Sélo et al. (2020) reported comparable as-built values of 119 ± 5 W·m⁻¹·K⁻¹ in the build direction and 103 ± 5 W·m⁻¹·K⁻¹ in the transverse direction (selo2020onthethermal pages 1-2, selo2020onthethermal pages 2-3). The reduced conductivity relative to pure aluminium (~237 W·m⁻¹·K⁻¹) is attributed to the supersaturated Si in the α-Al matrix and the fine Si cellular network that acts as an electron–phonon interface resistance (azizi2023processdependentanisotropicthermal pages 2-3). Butler et al. (2021) used a Wiedemann–Franz approach (four-wire electrical resistivity at 20 °C, Lorenz number L = 2.1 × 10⁻⁸ WΩ/K², phonon term k_g ≈ 10.5–13.6 W·m⁻¹·K⁻¹) and extrapolated the zero-porosity dense-material conductivity to 143.9 W·m⁻¹·K⁻¹ as-built and 191.5 W·m⁻¹·K⁻¹ after annealing (butler2021effectsofprocessing pages 4-5, butler2021effectsofprocessing pages 7-9).

**Effect of heat treatment.** All post-processing heat treatments increase the thermal conductivity by precipitating Si from the supersaturated matrix and coarsening the cellular Si network. Butler et al. found a 18–41% increase after annealing at 300–500 °C for 1–5 h, with 300 °C for 2 h being nearly sufficient for maximum improvement; porosity was unchanged (butler2021effectsofprocessing pages 1-2, butler2021effectsofprocessing pages 7-9). Sélo et al. reported that a 300 °C/2 h anneal raised conductivity to 173 ± 10 W·m⁻¹·K⁻¹ in both directions (anisotropy eliminated), a solution treatment at 520 °C gave +36%, and a T6-like cycle (520 °C/1 h + WQ + 160 °C/6 h) gave the largest increase at +44% (selo2020onthethermal pages 1-2, selo2020onthethermal pages 2-3). Liu et al. (2026) demonstrated that direct aging at 200 °C for 10 h (measured by LFA 447 laser flash) achieved 173.70 W·m⁻¹·K⁻¹, a 44.3% improvement over the as-built state (liu2026synergisticenhancementof pages 2-5).

**Temperature-dependent data (RT to solidus).** A notable gap in the literature is that existing studies on LPBF AlSi10Mg report thermal conductivity predominantly at room temperature. Temperature-dependent laser-flash data from room temperature up to the solidus (~555–570 °C for AlSi10Mg) specifically for LPBF-processed material were not found in the accessible literature. For modelling purposes, the temperature dependence of cast AlSi10Mg or AlSi12 may be used as a proxy, recognising that the LPBF microstructure will evolve (Si precipitation) during heating toward the solidus.
